ideas.title: Workout GC for Stalled Spec Homes
ideas.one_liner: A finish-the-house crew and re-sequencing service sold to construction lenders, not builders, for homes stuck at 40-90% complete.
ideas.customer: Community banks, credit unions and private construction lenders with spec-home loans being extended (Texas, Florida, Southeast, Mountain West). Secondary customer: distressed small builders referred by those lenders.
ideas.problem: Starts hold at 1.275M SAAR but completions fell 27.1% YoY. One executive described 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks, and a West Virginia builder risks about 40 closings. The builder cannot get crews back, and the lender holds the real risk: exhausted interest reserves, mechanic's liens, extensions, and half-built collateral. Lenders have no operating arm.
ideas.solution: Start with a flat-fee stuck-loan triage: site visit, photo scan, cost-to-finish, days of carry and sub availability, ranked across the lender's watchlist. Then take over scheduling and finishing on cost-plus. A few in-house supers plus a pre-vetted bench of framing, MEP and finish subs are paid in 7 days through the lender's normal draw process. The builder keeps the lot and the sale. A bonus is paid per day saved before the extension deadline.
ideas.why_now: Completions are down 27.1% while starts hold. 63% of builders already use incentives and 35% cut prices, so there is no margin left to absorb delay. ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026 and are pulling crews off sites. 2027 starts are forecast down 2-4%, so more small builders will stall. The 2024-25 vintage of spec construction loans is maturing now.
ideas.revenue_model: $2.5K per-loan triage or $15K portfolio review. Finishing work at cost plus 12-15%. Success fee of about 1% of loan balance for closing before the extension deadline.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames stalled homes as a builder or labor problem. The party with the budget, the legal leverage and no ego is the lender, who cares about loan resolution rather than building. Subs return when someone credible promises six straight days of work and pays in a week. A lender-backed GC has that payment credibility and the stalled builder does not.
ideas.first_30_days: Call 15 construction lenders and workout officers through state bankers associations. Offer two banks a free 10-loan triage. Hire two ex-superintendents. Line up 3 framing, MEP and finish subs per metro on a 7-day-pay promise. Target a first paid contract on 1-3 homes by day 30.

ideas.title: Part-Time Retired Journeymen as Apprentice Supervisors
ideas.one_liner: Supervision-as-a-service: retired licensed tradespeople work 2-3 days a week as the supervising journeyman that lets small shops deploy the apprentices and helpers they already have.
ideas.customer: 5-25 employee electrical, plumbing and HVAC shops with unlicensed helpers or apprentices, starting in one state with clear ratio and qualifier rules. They pay by the hour.
ideas.problem: The headlines say the pipeline is the shortage, but the Gen Z enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage. For many shops the binding constraint is licensed supervision, because ratio rules cap helpers per journeyman. Data-center overtime ($130-170K for journeymen, vendor stat) pulls supervisors off residential work. ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, yet retirees hold exactly the scarce credential and are unused.
ideas.solution: A vetted, insured bench of retired journeymen and masters placed part-time in shops as supervising journeyman and mentor. The platform verifies licenses, runs employer-of-record or 1099 structure per state rules, handles workers' comp, and automates the apprenticeship hour logs boards require. Shops book blocks such as Tue-Thu 7-3.
ideas.why_now: ABC's 2026 gap of 349K is mostly retirement. Data centers now account for nearly a third of the shortage. Immigration enforcement removes helpers, so shops need to hire and supervise local apprentices fast. Trade-school hype is masking a thin pipeline.
ideas.revenue_model: Shops pay about $75-110 per hour billed. The platform keeps 20-25% and the retiree keeps the rest. Add $150-250 per month for hour-logging and compliance software.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not labor, it is supervision minutes, and retirees want 16-hour weeks that no normal employer offers. A supervising journeyman unlocks one or two helpers billing at journeyman-adjacent rates, so shops can pay a premium and still gain margin. Rules vary by state and must be verified before launch.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one trade (electrical) in one state with clear ratio rules. Recruit 15 retirees from union retiree groups and lapsing-license lists. Sign 5 shops with 3+ helpers who are idle or under-deployed. Bill the first hours in week 3.

ideas.title: Half-Pro Remodeling: Homeowner Does the Easy 60%
ideas.one_liner: Fixed-price booking of only the licensed, permit-required slice of a project while homeowners or handymen do demo, prep and finish, with photo-verified handoffs.
ideas.customer: Budget-constrained homeowners with $3-15K bath, kitchen, water-heater, mini-split and electrical projects. Supply side: solo licensed plumbers and electricians who want prequalified, ready-to-work half-day jobs.
ideas.problem: Angi data shows 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects and 72% of postponers cite budget. The average project is $5,368. DIY-only fell from 50% to 39% while homeowner-plus-pro rose from 27% to 46%. Pros say they are too busy and skip small, messy, scope-uncertain jobs. Platforms sell whole jobs, so homeowners get no quotes.
ideas.solution: A catalog of standardized pro steps: rough-in for a vanity swap, shutoff valve and supply lines, gas line, water heater swap, ceiling-fan or lighting circuit, mini-split hookup, permit pull and inspection sign-off. Each comes with a homeowner checklist (nine prep steps, three photos) checked by a vision model, and a pro shows up for a fixed price to a job that is actually ready. Start only where owner-builder and licensing rules are clear.
ideas.why_now: Angi's 2026 backlog data. Credit cards rose to 30% of project payments. 62% now choose repair over replace. Contractors are capacity-constrained. Multimodal models can verify prep photos cheaply.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-20% take on the pro-step price ($300-1,500), plus materials affiliate margin from a local supply house. Pros pay nothing upfront.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The unit of demand is not the project, it is the licensed hour. The blended-work data says homeowners do not want turnkey, they want to transfer risk only on the parts they legally or practically cannot do. Nobody sells the licensed two hours with a photo-checked handoff, and small pros love the productivity of arriving at a ready job.
ideas.first_30_days: One metro, four job types. Recruit 10 solo plumbers and electricians from local trade Facebook groups. Launch a landing page with local ads. Run 30 bookings by hand with a spreadsheet and Stripe.

ideas.title: Supply-House-Branded Back Office for Tiny Shops
ideas.one_liner: White-label quote, invoice, parts-pricing and trade-credit software delivered to solo-to-5-tech shops through their local independent supply house counter.
ideas.customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical and roofing supply houses and regional distributors squeezed by Home Depot (SRS, GMS, Mingledorff's) and Lowe's (FBM, Artisan). End users are their trade account holders.
ideas.problem: ServiceTitan fell about 26% after Q2 on slowing GTV, softer HVAC leads and a delay on exteriors, and expects only about 700 locations on its agentic tier. Most tiny shops have no operations layer and will not buy software cold, since CAC is brutal and churn high. Independent distributors are losing pro accounts to big-box integration and need a reason for contractors to stay.
ideas.solution: A private-label 'contractor OS' under the distributor's brand. Quotes are built from the distributor's live price book, invoices are text-to-pay, job notes and callbacks are tracked, truck stock reorders route to the counter, and net-30 parts credit is bundled. Counter staff onboard shops in person. It is free with a trade account, and the distributor pays per active shop.
ideas.why_now: Home Depot bought Mingledorff's in May 2026 on top of SRS and GMS, and Lowe's bought FBM for $8.8B. Independents' backs are against the wall. ServiceTitan's drop and deprioritization of exteriors leave small shops ignored. LLM-assisted development makes a lightweight tool cheap to build.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-60 per active shop per month paid by the distributor, or 0.25-0.5% of the shop's parts spend. Add payments interchange share and parts-financing spread.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Vertical software wins on distribution. The supply house counter is the one place every tiny shop shows up every week, and distributors have both a strategic reason (defense against big-box) and a budget to pay for stickiness. Contractors will adopt anything that makes parts pricing and credit easier.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses through buying-group contacts. Build an MVP on price-book CSV upload, SMS quotes and Stripe. Pilot with 20 shops per distributor and measure parts spend lift per shop.

ideas.title: Reverse-Angi: Shops Sell Their Overflow Jobs
ideas.one_liner: Missed calls and too-busy jobs get routed to a trusted peer shop that pays the originating shop a referral fee.
ideas.customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and handyman shops with 1-15 techs in one metro, organized in trade circles that already vouch for each other.
ideas.problem: About 48% of home-services calls never reach a person (Invoca). Homeowners cite too-busy (21%) and no-response (14%) as barriers to hiring. Angi charges $15-85 per lead that is shared with many bidders, so shops distrust lead-gen. AI receptionists are crowded and merely take messages a shop cannot service.
ideas.solution: Shops forward busy, after-hours or out-of-scope calls to a number that answers in seconds, qualifies the job and offers it to the best-matched peer with capacity today. The job is transferred as an exclusive, pre-qualified lead. The originating shop earns a referral share of the invoice and the receiving shop pays a platform fee. Trust comes from peer vouching and network ratings. Cross-trade referrals (plumber to HVAC to electrician) are included.
ideas.why_now: In a labor-short market capacity is scarcer than demand: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects. Lead-gen distrust is high and ServiceTitan is moving upmarket. Real-time voice AI now handles triage well enough to answer instantly.
ideas.revenue_model: 20% of transferred-job revenue paid by the receiving shop, split about 10% to the originating shop and 10% to the platform. No subscription, so no adoption friction.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a labor-short market leads are not scarce, capacity is. Every busy shop is currently throwing away leads, so turn each shop from a lead buyer into a lead seller. It inverts Angi's economics: shops earn money for the calls they cannot take.
ideas.first_30_days: Seed 25 shops in one metro through local association groups. Use a Twilio number and a human dispatcher first. Settle via ACH. Track transfers and conversions weekly.

ideas.title: Pay-on-Pass: Inspections Trigger Sub Payments
ideas.one_liner: Same-day payment to framers and foundation crews the moment the city inspection clears, financed against the builder's draw.
ideas.customer: Small private builders (20-300 homes a year) and their framing, foundation, plumbing and electrical subs, with a community lender or credit line as funding partner.
ideas.problem: Cities adopt AI plan review, filings surge (Honolulu applications +34% but permits issued +5%, backlog 9,252), and the bottleneck moves to post-permit inspections. Subs wait for the pass, then wait for payment: one in five subs waits 60+ days and GCs are 4x more likely than subs to be paid within 30 days. Crews are already vanishing, so slow payers lose them.
ideas.solution: A payment rail keyed to a third-party-verified milestone: inspection status pulled from municipal portals or a photo of the green tag. The sub is paid within 24 hours from a revolving credit facility, repaid from the builder's draw within 30 days. Builders also get a crew reliability ranking and inspection-queue analytics by jurisdiction and inspector, with photo pre-checks to raise first-time pass rates.
ideas.why_now: AI permitting is deploying now (Honolulu, Denver's $4.6M contract), shifting the constraint downstream. Immigration enforcement makes verified crews scarce, so pay speed has become a recruiting tool. Completions are down 27.1%.
ideas.revenue_model: 1.5-2.5% of released payments, paid by the builder for speed and crew retention, with an optional sub-paid instant-pay discount. Spread on credit line usage.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The inspection pass is the only moment in construction that is third-party verified, timestamped and dispute-proof, which makes it the ideal payment trigger and collateral. Nobody uses it because the data sits in thousands of scattered municipal portals, but one builder in one metro needs only three or four.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro and its three permit portals. Pilot with 3 builders and their 5 framing and foundation subs. Open a $100-200K line with a friendly community lender. Verify passes by hand and pay by ACH.

ideas.title: Remote Load Calcs That Avoid Panel Upgrades
ideas.one_liner: A photo-and-utility-bill service that proves an existing electrical panel can take a heat pump or EV charger, with load-management devices when it cannot.
ideas.customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger installers and solar-plus-storage installers without in-house electricians. Later: state and utility electrification programs.
ideas.problem: Data centers are absorbing electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months). Residential electrician time becomes the scarcest input, so panel upgrades stall every electrification job. HVAC contractors selling heat pumps are blocked by work they do not do and cannot schedule. The HVAC rebound expected in 2027 will make it worse.
ideas.solution: Installer uploads a photo of the panel label plus 12 months of utility data. The service returns a permit-ready load calculation under the existing-load method, stamped by a remote licensed engineer or electrician. It recommends the cheapest path: no upgrade, a load-management or circuit-pausing device allowed by recent NEC editions, or a smart panel, with the material list for the installer's quote.
ideas.why_now: Electrician scarcity from data-center overtime ($130-170K, vendor stat), 2027 HVAC rebound with A2L certification adding friction, and a 110K technician shortage. Load-management devices and energy-management provisions are now commercially available and code-recognized in many places.
ideas.revenue_model: $79-149 per calculation billed to installers. Annual contracts with programs. Referral margin from load-management device makers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for electrification is neither the heat pump nor the HVAC tech, it is the panel and the electrician-days it consumes. Avoiding electrician hours is worth more than adding them, and the existing truck-roll panel check can be done as a $99 desk job by one remote engineer serving many installers.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 20 HVAC contractors in one state. Contract a licensed PE or master electrician for templates and stamps. Deliver 50 calculations by hand. Measure the percentage that avoided an upgrade.

ideas.title: All-In Site Quotes for Chassis-Free Homes
ideas.one_liner: Type a parcel address, get a fixed-price foundation, utility-hookup and permit package for a factory-built home, delivered by a local crew network.
ideas.customer: Manufactured and modular home dealers, small landowners and buyers, and factory builders that need site-work partners. Rural and small-town jurisdictions benefit indirectly.
ideas.problem: The ROAD to Housing Act (signed July 11, 2026) kills the steel-chassis rule, worth about $10K or 10% of unit cost, though HUD must still publish standards. Cheaper units will ship, but the sale is decided by unknown site costs: foundation, utilities, septic or well, set crew and permits. These stay local and human, and dealers cannot quote the all-in price.
ideas.solution: A parcel-level site-cost estimator using soils, flood zone, utility distance, jurisdiction fees and foundation type, returning a fixed-price quote in 24 hours. It is backed by a vetted crew network (excavation, foundation, set, utilities) on 7-day pay, one accountable contract, and packaged construction-to-perm financing. Begin with conventional manufactured homes on permanent foundations, so revenue starts before HUD standards land.
ideas.why_now: ROAD Act enacted July 2026 with HUD standards pending and a federal showcase of factory-built homes. Site work is exactly where the labor shortage and permit friction bite hardest. Standard duplex and townhome blueprints are being funded.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-15% GC margin on site packages ($30-60K). $300-500 quote fee credited on booking. Dealer referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone watching the ROAD Act watches factories and financing. The bottleneck will be the last 100 feet, and price uncertainty there kills the cheap-home pitch. The first team that gives a real all-in number becomes the dealers' default site partner and captures the margin the factory cannot.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose a county cluster in Texas or the Southeast where manufactured homes are common. Sign two dealers. Build the estimator from public GIS, flood and utility data. Deliver 20 free quotes and convert 2-3 to jobs with existing subs.

ideas.title: Investor-Cap Look-Through Checks for Title Companies
ideas.one_liner: An API that traces a buyer's LLC web to its parent and counts the homes it controls, so title and escrow can clear the ROAD Act's 350-home limit at closing.
ideas.customer: Title and escrow companies, closing attorneys and lenders in single-family-heavy metros. Secondary: mid-size investors (100-349 homes) who need to stay under the cap and prove it.
ideas.problem: The ROAD Act bars investors with more than 350 homes from buying existing houses. Compliance depends on affiliate holdings scattered across thousands of LLCs, which the closing agent cannot see. Large buyers will restructure into fragments, and mid-size investors suddenly need to manage headroom. Who is liable when a closing clears wrongly is unresolved.
ideas.solution: Entity resolution across county deed records, Secretary of State filings, registered-agent and address graphs and mailing addresses. It returns a portfolio count with a confidence score in seconds, an audit-ready evidence file for the closing, and a headroom dashboard for investors near the cap. Verify statute text, effective date, affiliate definition and exemptions first.
ideas.why_now: The law took effect in July 2026, and implementation questions are open now. Title agents are the natural chokepoint, as they already collect ownership details on entity purchases. Entity-resolution tooling and cheaper county record access make a small-team build feasible.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40 per buyer-entity check. $500-2,000 per month SaaS for investors. Enterprise licenses to title underwriters.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The people obligated to comply cannot compute the answer, and the people who can compute it are not in the transaction. The closing desk becomes the enforcement point, and mid-size investors treat their 350th home as a scarce budget, creating a second buyer for the same data.
ideas.first_30_days: Build for three metros where large single-family operators concentrate. Ingest deed and Secretary of State data. Sell paid pilots to 5 title agencies and 2 underwriters. Publish a free entity-count explainer to attract inbound.

ideas.title: Closing-Risk Radar for New-Construction Loan Officers
ideas.one_liner: Forecasts which locked new-build closings will miss their rate-lock window, using permit and inspection data plus builder history, so loan officers extend cheaply or re-price before the buyer walks.
ideas.customer: New-construction loan officers and mortgage teams (builder-preferred lenders, community banks), title companies, and small builders' sales managers.
ideas.problem: 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns, and completions fell 27.1% as crews vanish, foundations sit idle and electricians are delayed up to 2 months. Closing dates slip, locks expire and buydown funding is stranded. A West Virginia builder is at risk of losing about 40 closings. Nobody forecasts construction slippage, only rates.
ideas.solution: For each locked loan, ingest the address and pull permit and inspection status from municipal portals, add the builder's stage photos or one-question SMS replies, and output a slip probability and the cheapest date to extend. Add a monthly builder reliability scorecard for lender risk and builder-relations teams.
ideas.why_now: Buydown-dependent sales, mortgage rates near 7%, falling completions and forecast 2027 starts down 2-4% mean lock-expiry losses will climb. LLM-based extraction from messy municipal portals is now cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-50 per monitored loan or $400-800 per month per loan officer. Enterprise scorecards for lender risk teams.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Loan officers care about the construction calendar as much as the rate curve, and they have direct fee income at stake when a lock lapses, unlike builders who learn late. Public inspection sequence is a surprisingly strong predictor of slip, and the reliability scorecard is a byproduct with its own buyer.
ideas.first_30_days: Sell to five new-construction loan officers in Texas and the Southeast. Each shares 20-40 pending closings. Build the forecast manually in spreadsheets from portals and show five saves in 30 days.

ideas.title: Tariff Exposure Radar by House Plan
ideas.one_liner: A per-plan bill-of-materials scan that flags the small imported, tariff-exposed slice of inputs, prices the swing and proposes lower-exposure substitutes.
ideas.customer: Purchasing managers and owners at regional and mid-size builders (100-2,000 homes a year), remodelers, and building-material dealers. Distribution via home builders associations.
ideas.problem: NAHB estimates tariffs add $10,900 per home and Brookings sees about $30B added to residential construction and renovation cost by 2027. Only about 7% of inputs are imported, but they are mostly items with no quick domestic substitute, and reported lumber and steel tariff rates conflict across sources. Builders reprice by gut, sign fixed-price contracts blind, and have no per-plan exposure number.
ideas.solution: Ingest plan takeoffs and supplier price lists, map each SKU to country of origin and tariff line, and compute exposure per plan and per option package. Deliver escalation-clause language for buyer and sub contracts, alerts when rates change, substitute suggestions from domestic or alternate-origin catalogs, and a group-buy on substitutes.
ideas.why_now: Tariff rates are moving and sources disagree. Builder margins are gone (63% use incentives), so a $10K per-home swing decides whether a plan pencils. Structured plan data is now available from design-automation tools.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-2,000 per month per builder. $1,500 one-off plan audits. 2-4% rebate on substituted spend from group buys.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Because most of a house is domestic, the tariff burden is a short list of SKUs, so the right tool is a narrow, boring lookup rather than a global trade-compliance platform. The money is in plan-level re-spec and escalation clauses, not in customs filings.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer 10 builders a free top-40 exposed-SKU audit from their last three takeoffs and supplier quotes. Send a one-page report and convert 3 to paid. Get a slot in a regional builders association newsletter.

ideas.title: Pre-Cut Electrical Kits Per House Plan
ideas.one_liner: A regional kitting shop ships each production home's wiring as pre-cut, labeled, bundled kits so a helper pulls and a journeyman only terminates and inspects.
ideas.customer: Electrical subcontractors serving production and spec builders (5-100 homes a year), and builders in data-center-hot markets such as Texas.
ideas.problem: Data centers absorb electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; journeymen on overtime gross $130-170K, vendor stat), and Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months. Meanwhile much rough-in time goes to measuring, cutting and pulling, which does not need a licensed person's minutes.
ideas.solution: For each repeat plan, generate a wire schedule and build kits: cable pre-cut and labeled by room and circuit, boxes pre-assembled, home runs pre-bundled, panel schedule pre-printed, delivered in numbered bins by phase. Lower-skill pullers or apprentices do most of the rough-in under supervision, and the journeyman terminates and inspects.
ideas.why_now: Electrician arbitrage from data-center overtime, builders with idle houses waiting on electrical, and digital plan libraries that expose structured circuit data. Wire-processing machines are cheap and used equipment is plentiful.
ideas.revenue_model: Materials plus 15-25%, or $2-4K per home, with a share of labor savings. Licensing the process to kitting shops in other metros.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is journeyman minutes on tasks a journeyman does not need to do. Commercial contractors have prefabbed for decades, but residential never did because labor was cheap, and now the ROI is large.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one production builder's most repeated plan. Hire an ex-electrician estimator and buy or rent a used cut-and-label machine. Sell kits for five homes to the builder's electrical sub and measure hours saved per house.

ideas.title: Tech-to-Owner Buyout Kit for Trade Shops
ideas.one_liner: Package and finance the sale of sub-$5M trade shops to their own senior technicians or managers, then keep them on a shared back office so the acquired shop does not stall.
ideas.customer: Retiring owners of 5-40 person HVAC, plumbing, electrical and roofing shops that PE roll-ups skip, plus their number-two techs or GMs and SBA lenders.
ideas.problem: McKinsey says 6M small businesses face ownership transitions by 2035 and a third of owners over 50 struggle to find a buyer. PE pays 10-14x EBITDA for platforms above $25M revenue but only 2-3.5x for small owner-operators, a 3-5x valuation gap. When the small shop closes, its crew and customers vanish, deepening the trades shortage.
ideas.solution: A deal factory: clean financials from QuickBooks and field-service exports, SBA 7(a) plus seller-note packaging, a 90-day transition playbook, license-qualifier continuity, and a fractional-CFO and shared back office (payroll, purchasing group, bidding) for the new owner. A short cohort teaches buyer-techs finance, hiring and pricing.
ideas.why_now: PE buying spree (Apollo/Apex, Blackstone/Champions, Bain/Service Logic) raises the visible price of scale but skips small shops. The silver-tsunami timeline is now. Roofing is the least consolidated trade and ServiceTitan is deprioritizing it, so owners have fewer software-led growth options.
ideas.revenue_model: 3-5% success fee on the deal. $2-4K per month shared back-office subscription for 24-36 months.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The best buyer for a small shop is not PE or a stranger, it is the employee who already knows the customers, trucks and quirks. What is missing is packaging, seller financing and post-close operating support. Every closed shop deletes 5-20 tradespeople from a scarce local supply, which makes preservation valuable to the community.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one trade in one metro. Cold-outreach 200 owners aged 58+ from state license databases with a free 30-minute valuation chat. Sign three exclusive listings, identify the tech buyers via the owners, and line up two SBA lenders.

ideas.title: Fast-Pay Administrator for Funded Home Repair
ideas.one_liner: Run the paperwork and pay small contractors in days on grant- and program-funded repairs (weatherization, aging-in-place, municipal repair programs) where waitlists exist because few pros will bid.
ideas.customer: Nonprofits, community action agencies, Area Agencies on Aging, housing authorities and municipal home-repair programs with budgets but weak execution capacity.
ideas.problem: Programs have money but not throughput: jobs are small ($2-15K), paperwork-heavy (income verification, lead-safe rules, photos, inspections) and reimbursed in 30-90 days. Good contractors are too busy for low-margin, slow-pay work. The median home is 44 years old, repair-over-replace is at 62%, and homeowners cannot get quotes.
ideas.solution: Act as general contractor of record plus payment desk: take the program's approved scope, match it to vetted small pros, run documentation and inspections in a phone workflow, pay the pro in 5-7 days by fronting cash, and bill the agency with audit-ready files. The agency's program-delivery budget line pays the admin fee.
ideas.why_now: Aging housing stock and record remodeling spend ($524B) mean small pros have plenty of alternatives to slow-pay work. Vision and document models make photo-based compliance cheap. Slower remodeling growth (about 1.6% by year-end) should free some pro capacity for steady program work.
ideas.revenue_model: 12-18% admin fee on job value paid by the agency, plus a 1-2% factoring spread on advances.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In public repair programs the scarce input is neither money nor eligible homeowners, it is good contractors' willingness to endure paperwork and slow pay. Fast payment plus document automation is the moat, and the customer already has a budget line for program delivery.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach five agencies with waitlists in one state. Offer a 10-job cost-plus pilot. Recruit 10 small pros on a 7-day-pay promise. Open a $75K working-capital line and run documentation through simple phone forms.

ideas.title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
ideas.one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
ideas.customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
ideas.problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
ideas.solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
ideas.why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
ideas.revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

ideas.title: Insurer-Backed Self-Certified Permits for ADUs
ideas.one_liner: Japan-style private building confirmation: AI code review plus a licensed private reviewer plus an insurer-backed compliance warranty, so an ADU or small addition gets a certified package in about 48 hours where state law allows private providers.
ideas.customer: ADU builders, residential designers and architects, and homeowners in states with private-provider or third-party review statutes (Florida first), later cities piloting insured expedited review.
ideas.problem: Honolulu residential permits average 218 days (commercial 469). Government AI tools serve reviewers, and applicant-side tools for ADU owners, small builders and rural jurisdictions are thin. Faster review even increases filings (+34%) faster than permits issued (+5%).
ideas.solution: An applicant-side pre-clearance engine reads the plan set, runs the jurisdiction's zoning, structural and energy rules, and returns a correction list in minutes. A licensed private provider signs, and a surplus-lines policy from an MGA indemnifies owner and jurisdiction against code errors, priced from the engine's error data. Where private-provider laws exist the package is submitted directly, and elsewhere it is offered as an insured fast-track pilot.
ideas.why_now: Government pilots prove review can be automated (Honolulu review cycles down 58%, Denver's $4.6M contract). LLMs can now read plan sets. The ROAD Act funds standard blueprints. Insurers are hunting for new specialty lines, and applicants are desperate.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 per ADU permit package. 10-15% share of warranty premium. SaaS for designers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Governments will never build the applicant-side tool because of conflict of interest, but insurance can do what regulators cannot: price and carry the residual risk that a bad plan slips through. Japan has let designated private bodies issue building confirmations since the late 1990s, and permit timelines there are days, not months.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a Florida private-provider firm. Run 20 ADU and remodel plan sets free for three designers and compare predicted corrections to actual city comments. Pre-sell to ADU builders at $1,500 and show the accuracy data to two MGAs.

ideas.title: Teleoperated Trenching Crews for Infill Lots
ideas.one_liner: A control room of remote operators driving retrofitted compact excavators and skid steers on residential lots (utility trenching, pad grading, backfill), sold per linear foot.
ideas.customer: Small and ADU builders, factory-built home dealers needing site work, and small site-work contractors short on operators.
ideas.problem: Site work and foundations are the first constraint (foundations wait 30+ days; 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks). Operators are aging out and are poached by larger jobs. Small residential jobs waste an operator's day on travel and waiting.
ideas.solution: Rental compact excavators fitted with joystick actuation, cameras, cellular or satellite bonding and a geofence kill-switch. Operators, including 55+ or injured veterans, run machines from a control room, one job after another across a metro, while a local machine tender handles spotting and moves. Start with the lowest-risk tasks in fenced residential lots and sell by linear foot.
ideas.why_now: Teleoperation retrofit kits and satellite or 5G links are now off-the-shelf. Autonomous pile drivers already work commercially on solar sites, proving field-robot acceptance. Enforcement and the labor squeeze are thinning site crews.
ideas.revenue_model: $175-225 per operated machine-hour or per-linear-foot pricing. Retrofit and rental margin. Later, software licensing to sitework contractors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The unlock is not autonomy, which is hard, but operator pooling. A person on site wastes half a day traveling and idling, whereas a remote operator can serve many small jobs, and older or injured operators can keep working. Small lots become profitable.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent one compact excavator and buy a retrofit or factory remote kit. Test in a closed lot with a safety case and insurance broker input. Sign 3 ADU or factory-home dealers for trenching on fenced lots. Run the first paid jobs with a spotter present.

ideas.title: Crawlspace Robots for the 44-Year-Old House
ideas.one_liner: Small tracked robots that scan, photograph and eventually air-seal and insulate the crawlspaces and attics humans dread, starting as a quote-enabling survey service.
ideas.customer: Home inspectors, insurers and home-warranty firms (moisture and water-damage claims), and HVAC, insulation and foundation-repair contractors who need access before quoting. Later: weatherization programs.
ideas.problem: Median home age is 44 years, 62% of homeowners now choose repair over replace, and 78% of those with unstarted projects have no quotes. Contractors avoid the crawlspace visit because it is slow, dirty and unsafe, so inspectors skip it and quotes are guesses. It is the most avoided labor in the house.
ideas.solution: Phase 1: a low-cost tracked robot with camera, thermal and LiDAR plus a vision-language pipeline producing a 10-minute survey covering moisture, insulation, duct leaks, pest and mold signs and structural issues, sold as an add-on to inspectors and a pre-quote survey to contractors. Phase 2: tool attachments for air sealing and topping insulation. Phase 3: crawlspace-as-a-service retrofit fleet.
ideas.why_now: Cheap edge compute, reliable vision-language defect classification and low-cost thermal sensors. Labor shortages make anyone willing to crawl scarce. Insurers want moisture data and aging stock keeps growing.
ideas.revenue_model: $149-249 per survey (inspector add-on or contractor pre-quote), insurer report fees, later per-job retrofit revenue.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The robot does not need to replace skilled trades, only the worst 20 minutes of their job. Access is the friction, and a proprietary library of real crawlspace conditions is the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Build v0 from a hobby tracked chassis, action camera and thermal sensor (about $3K). Run 30 free surveys for 5 home inspectors and 2 insulation contractors. Track how often findings convert to jobs and test pricing.

ideas.title: Screw-Pile Foundations That Skip the Concrete Crew
ideas.one_liner: Engineered helical-pile foundations with torque-logged QA and prefab floor cassettes, installed in a day, for spec homes, ADUs and factory-built homes where foundation crews are booked out for weeks.
ideas.customer: Spec and production builders in crew-constrained markets (Texas, Florida), ADU builders and factory-built home dealers.
ideas.problem: Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and loan interest keeps accruing while 15-20 houses wait 6+ weeks. Forming, pouring and finishing are crew-dependent and hard to automate. Chassis-free factory homes need light foundations that are quick to install.
ideas.solution: A foundation-only subcontractor installing helical piles with a torque-monitoring logger and structural details pre-approved by a partner engineer for three soil regions, plus a prefab insulated floor cassette or steel grade beam. Torque logs become an objective, timestamped QA report for inspectors and lenders. Autonomous pile driving, already proven in solar, is the roadmap.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement and labor shortages are stretching foundation crews. Autonomous pile-driving rigs are commercial in solar. Chassis-free homes and the ADU boom create demand for light foundations. Lenders and inspectors increasingly accept digital QA data.
ideas.revenue_model: Priced roughly at parity with slab or stem-wall per home and sold on speed, with margin from utilization. Per-sq-ft or per-home pricing, plus licensing engineered details to other installers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Changing the design removes the scarce trade from the critical path entirely. Insiders try to hire or automate concrete crews, but a foundation with no forms, no cure time and no finishers becomes a machine-and-engineering task with objective logs.
ideas.first_30_days: Engage a geotech and a structural PE for standard details. Rent a mini-excavator with a torque head. Sign two builders with stuck lots or ADUs, install three foundations, and document schedule savings versus their alternatives.

ideas.title: Exoskeletons That Delay Tradesperson Retirement
ideas.one_liner: Lease passive and powered exoskeletons with fitting, coaching and outcome-based pricing to shops and insurers, targeting 55+ tradespeople whose retirement drives the labor gap.
ideas.customer: Workers' comp carriers and PEOs, contractor associations, and 10-100 employee roofing, plumbing, HVAC, framing and drywall shops with aging crews.
ideas.problem: ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, and older tradespeople leave over knees, backs and shoulders. Replacement hiring is impossible in a market where trade-school enrollment hype is called a demographic mirage. Strain injuries also drive comp claims.
ideas.solution: Vetted kits (passive shoulder and back supports, emerging powered hip and knee assists), professional fitting, a task playbook for overhead, attic, roofing and crawlspace work, and usage and injury-risk telemetry. Monthly lease with a guarantee tied to comp premium reduction or absence rates, piloted with carriers first.
ideas.why_now: Powered assist suits have fallen from tens of thousands of dollars to low thousands per unit. Comp carriers face margin pressure and want proven loss-control tools. The retirement wave now dominates the labor gap, and hiring cannot fill it.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-300 per worker per month lease, a carrier program fee, and outcome-based rebates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is a retention and insurance business, not a robotics business: the cheapest new journeyman is the 62-year-old who did not retire. The buyer with the incentive and the loss data is the comp carrier, not the worker or the owner.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach two regional comp carriers or PEOs with a 60-day pilot. Sign three shops (10 workers total) and measure discomfort, absences and adoption. Secure wholesale terms with one exoskeleton supplier and one trade association endorsement.

ideas.title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Downstream Payers
ideas.one_liner: Recover itemized tariff surcharges from suppliers who were refunded the tariffs, on contingency, and give surcharge-collecting firms a defensive ledger.
ideas.customer: Small contractors, restaurants, repair shops and retailers who were invoiced a separate 'tariff surcharge' line by suppliers in 2025-26, plus small firms that added such surcharges to their own customers' bills.
ideas.problem: SCOTUS ruled on 2026-02-20 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, and about $166B in CBP refunds go to the importer of record (about $81B paid by July). Over 40% of small firms saw tariff cost increases and 76% of international sourcers passed them on, so the firm that paid the pass-through gets nothing. Each claim is too small ($200-$8k) for a lawyer, and firms that billed surcharges to their own customers now carry their own exposure.
ideas.solution: Read-only scan of the owner's mailbox and QuickBooks/Xero pulls every tariff or surcharge line from vendor invoices and from the firm's own customer invoices. It builds a two-sided surcharge ledger (paid upstream, collected downstream), then generates supplier demand letters that cite the invoice wording and contract terms. Unpaid claims escalate to small-claims templates or a partner attorney. Claims are strongest where the invoice said the surcharge was itemized or refundable. Because one supplier can owe hundreds of customers, settlements can be negotiated per supplier instead of per claim.
ideas.why_now: Refunds have been flowing through CBP's automated system since April 2026, so suppliers are holding refund cash right now, before it is absorbed into margins. Invoice records are fresh and 2026 books have not closed.
ideas.revenue_model: 25-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a $49 flat fee for the ledger and audit. Later, a per-supplier settlement-program fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Refund law is written for importers, but the money trail is an invoice trail. Itemized invoices are contract evidence, and thousands of tiny claims against a few hundred suppliers form a portfolio no law firm will touch. The same ledger doubles as a defense file for firms that billed surcharges.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer a free 'surcharge audit' in trade-specific Facebook groups and subreddits (HVAC, restaurant equipment, apparel resellers). Hand-review 50 mailboxes and find the 10 suppliers with the most itemized surcharges. Retain a consumer-protection attorney to review the demand-letter template, send the first 100 letters, and measure the response rate.

ideas.title: Supplier-Funded Books for Trade-Credit Customers
ideas.one_liner: Regional distributors pay to give each micro-customer done-for-you books, and get a permissioned live view of that customer's credit risk.
ideas.customer: Regional wholesale distributors (foodservice, produce, beauty supply, auto parts, building materials, uniform and linen) with 500-10,000 micro accounts on net-30 terms.
ideas.problem: Distributors extend trade credit to taquerias, salons and garages on gut feel, and bad debt and slow pay eat margin. Micro-customers keep no books, so there is no data to underwrite against. Ramp and Brex have moved upmarket and no vendor serves this tier. The owners will not pay for bookkeeping themselves.
ideas.solution: Every active account gets free, done-for-you books, funded by the distributor. Bank and card feeds are connected, the distributor's own invoices are auto-ingested, and receipts arrive by text or WhatsApp. The customer owns the ledger and can export it any time. With the customer's opt-in, the distributor sees cash coverage, the aging of the customer's other bills and payment-risk flags, and can raise limits or offer early-pay discounts to accounts that look healthy.
ideas.why_now: LLM categorization pushes cost per account below about $10 a month. The Fed's 2026 data shows microfirms are cash-tight (22% of applicants got no financing, and nonemployers lean on personal funds). The Bench collapse made data ownership and portability a selling point.
ideas.revenue_model: The distributor pays $10-25 per active account per month, justified by bad-debt reduction, shorter DSO and lower churn. Upsells: tax filing, payroll, and early-payment financing with a revenue share.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The micro-business will never pay for bookkeeping, but the party carrying its receivable will. A bad account costs a distributor thousands, while $15 a month is noise. Sponsorship also raises switching costs, so the distributor gets retention for free.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one vertical in one metro, such as a produce or beauty-supply distributor. Get 12 months of invoices and payment history for 100 accounts, then backtest whether simple books-derived signals predict late payment. Sign a paid pilot covering 100 accounts, with success defined as DSO and write-offs.

ideas.title: Price-Raise Autopilot for One-Person Service Firms
ideas.one_liner: Find the underpriced clients in a solo operator's own invoice history and execute personalized price increases, paid as a share of the uplift.
ideas.customer: Nonemployer and 1-5 person service businesses with 50-800 repeat clients: groomers, cleaners, landscapers, bookkeepers, tutors, therapists, detailers.
ideas.problem: Rising costs are the top financial challenge, yet most solo operators have not repriced in years because they fear churn. The industry sells lead generation, not repricing, even though a modest increase on the bottom 40% of clients often beats a 20% lift in leads.
ideas.solution: Connect Stripe, Square, QuickBooks, Jobber or booking-software history. For each client, compute the effective hourly rate after drive time, materials and discounts, and rank clients as safe-to-raise or protect. Draft one-to-one messages in the owner's voice, send by text or email, track churn and replies, and roll back individual clients if needed. The dashboard shows before-and-after profit per hour.
ideas.why_now: The Fed's 2026 survey shows 76% of international sourcers already passed costs to customers, so consumers now accept increases. Payment and booking APIs give clean multi-year history, and LLMs write natural personal notes at zero marginal cost.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-20% of first-year incremental revenue captured (no uplift, no fee), or a $49/month plan for owners who prefer flat pricing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The industry assumes the number-one problem, getting customers, is the one to fix. For a business of one, the fastest path to profit is charging existing customers correctly, and owners are too close to their clients to do it themselves. Outcome pricing also works because the owner sees the money.
ideas.first_30_days: Run a concierge version for 20 groomers, cleaners and landscapers found in local Facebook groups, using exports and spreadsheets. Measure revenue lift and churn below 3%. Publish two before-and-after case studies and use them to price the software.

ideas.title: Sell the Route, Not the Business
ideas.one_liner: A standardized customer-book sale with a retention earn-out held in escrow and released automatically from payment data.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators aged 58+ of recurring-revenue routes with $80-500k revenue (pool, lawn, pest, cleaning, snow, window, HVAC maintenance, small bookkeeping and tax practices), and 5-30 employee competitors nearby who would buy them.
ideas.problem: No broker will list a $150k-revenue business, so retiring owners walk away and customers scatter. Buyers can't verify retention and the parties fight over price. Search funds target $5-50M companies and nothing serves the sub-$1M tier.
ideas.solution: Package the asset as the recurring customer relationship, not the entity. The product supplies consented customer-list transfer, a standard purchase agreement, a pricing multiple on trailing recurring revenue, and a 12-month retention earn-out held in escrow that releases as Stripe, QuickBooks or bank data confirms customers still pay. It adds customer-notice and handover-ride workflows, a non-compete, and matching to nearby operators. SBA Express lender partners finance the buyer.
ideas.why_now: From July 2026 an SBA 7(a) can be combined with a 504 for up to $10M, which loosens acquisition credit. Payment data now makes retention measurable in real time. An aging owner cohort meets flat CPA supply on the bookkeeping side.
ideas.revenue_model: 5-8% success fee to seller and buyer, plus escrow and retention-tracking fees, plus referral fees from lenders and insurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: At this size nobody needs to find a buyer for the business, because the natural buyer is the competitor with trucks two zip codes away. Retention escrow turns the valuation argument into a measured outcome.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose one vertical (for example pool routes) in one metro. Broker three deals by hand through Facebook groups and route-broker forums using a lawyer-drafted standard contract and Stripe Connect escrow. Document time to close and retention, then productize the paperwork.

ideas.title: Year-Round Books for Immigrant-Community Tax Storefronts
ideas.one_liner: Give community tax preparers WhatsApp-native, in-language AI bookkeeping so they can serve their small-business clients all year.
ideas.customer: Independent tax storefronts in Latino, Vietnamese, Korean, Chinese and other immigrant communities, each serving 100-500 micro-business clients (taquerias, nail salons, owner-operator truckers, cleaners, roofing crews) who show up with a shoebox once a year.
ideas.problem: The clients have no monthly books. Preparers can't do year-round bookkeeping without adding headcount, and they cannot afford Intuit's or H&R Block's offering. Silicon Valley assumes better AI will close the trust gap, but these owners trust a person who speaks their language.
ideas.solution: White-label intake through WhatsApp, WeChat or KakaoTalk: the client sends receipt photos and voice notes in their language, and AI drafts the ledger and a monthly P&L. The preparer reviews exceptions in a queue and sends a plain-language summary. Sales tax, payroll deposits and quarterly estimated tax reminders are included. All output carries the preparer's brand.
ideas.why_now: Multilingual and code-switched voice transcription became reliable in 2025-26. IRS Direct File ended for 2026, and Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices and 20 TurboTax storefronts, which suggests trust stays human and local.
ideas.revenue_model: $99/month per storefront plus $12 per client per month, or a 30% revenue share on a $150 per client monthly bookkeeping fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The trust problem is already solved by a human who is embedded in the community. What the preparer lacks is leverage, and the incumbents are hiring storefronts, not selling to them. AI turns a seasonal tax business into a year-round one.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10 storefronts in one metro through ITIN and tax-prep associations and Spanish-language radio. Pilot with five clients each on WhatsApp Business. Charge nothing until the storefronts see retention and added revenue, then set the per-client price.

ideas.title: Placement Exchange for Clients PE Firms Shed
ideas.one_liner: A compliant offboarding and warm-handoff service that places small clients dropped by PE-backed accounting firms with vetted independent bookkeepers.
ideas.customer: PE-backed and roll-up accounting platforms that raise fee minimums and prune small clients, and independent bookkeepers, enrolled agents and CPAs who want more clients.
ideas.problem: PE roll-ups push firms toward larger clients (prior knowledge, not re-verified), so thousands of micro-clients get a 30-day termination letter with scattered records. The exiting firm has E&O and reputation exposure, and the clients don't know where to go. Independent shops want clients but cannot find or vet them. CPA supply is flat at about 678,000.
ideas.solution: An offboarding workflow for the shedding firm: client consent, export of prior-year returns and workpapers, engagement-letter templates, and a warm handoff to independents matched on industry, software, language and location. Receiving firms are vetted and rated, and there is a service-level guarantee if the client is unhappy.
ideas.why_now: Multi-year PE consolidation of accounting firms continues, AI reduces cost-to-serve for large clients faster than small ones, and the CPA pipeline is flat while demand is projected to rise.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-400 per placed client from the receiving firm, $50-100 per client offboarding fee from the shedding firm, and later 8-10% of first-year fees as a recurring referral.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For the roll-up, shedding small clients is an unpriced cost center with legal exposure, so it will pay for graceful exits. The demand side is a waiting list of independents.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 independent bookkeepers and EAs as the buyer panel. Approach operations leaders at five regional roll-ups and offer a free pilot for 50 pruned clients. Build the export checklist and record acceptance and satisfaction rates.

ideas.title: Tip Provenance Ledger for Tipped-Occupation Employers
ideas.one_liner: An evidence trail that classifies every dollar as a voluntary tip, service charge, pool or cash tip, to support new tip-deduction reporting.
ideas.customer: Restaurants, bars, salons, spas, barbershops, valet operators, car washes and delivery fleets with 5-60 workers on Toast, Square, Clover or spreadsheets, and self-employed booth renters in tipped occupations.
ideas.problem: The 2025 reconciliation law made qualified tips and overtime deductible, and the IRS says employers must file information returns on them. Workers now have an incentive to relabel pay as tips. Owners must separate voluntary tips from mandatory service charges, pooled tips and cash tips, and errors trigger worker disputes and IRS letters.
ideas.solution: Ingest POS, payment and payroll data and tag each dollar with provenance. Produce the W-2 or 1099 support schedule, worker-facing statements so employees can claim their deduction, and an audit binder. Flag anomalies such as a service charge quietly recategorized as tips at year-end.
ideas.why_now: Tax year 2026 is the first full year under the new rules and W-2s are due January 31, 2027. Payroll vendors are adding fields but not provenance.
ideas.revenue_model: $29-79 per location per month, plus $3 per worker statement. Channel through POS app stores and restaurant bookkeepers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A deduction that is valuable to both worker and owner creates an incentive to reclassify, which makes the evidence trail the product, in the same way that exemption certificates support sales-tax deductions. Payroll vendors will add a field but not the audit trail.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 15 restaurants and salons through bookkeepers. Build a Square and Toast CSV importer and offer a free Q4 tip audit. Convert audit customers to an annual plan ahead of the W-2 deadline.

ideas.title: Business Identity Watch: LifeLock for LLCs
ideas.one_liner: Continuous monitoring of the state filings, liens and listings that define a small business, with a fast response kit when someone hijacks them.
ideas.customer: Owners of LLCs and sole proprietorships, reached through community banks, insurance agents, CPAs and registered-agent companies.
ideas.problem: Formation is cheap and online, and US domestic companies no longer file beneficial-ownership reports (FinCEN's final rule, August 2026). Census restated its formation series and excluded internet-sales-linked applications from some series, which suggests formation counts are polluted by non-real businesses (inference). Fraudsters can file fake officer or agent changes, register lookalike LLCs and domains, hijack listings and file bogus liens. Owners find out when a collections letter arrives.
ideas.solution: Monitor Secretary of State filings across states with open bulk feeds, UCC indexes, lookalike entity names and domains, and Google Business Profile edits. Alert the owner and provide pre-drafted correction filings, fraud affidavits, a registered-agent switch, and a bank notification letter.
ideas.why_now: There is no federal ownership registry to lean on, formation is cheap, and AI makes synthetic-identity and lookalike-business fraud cheaper to run.
ideas.revenue_model: $9-19 per entity per month, a $299 incident-response fee, and bulk banking deals at about $2 per entity per month.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The state filing is the root of trust for a small business, and nobody watches it. Identity-theft companies watch people, not entities, and a bank that already knows the business is the natural distributor.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick five states with open bulk filing data and build change alerts. Pilot with 200 LLCs through one community bank or bookkeeper. Track fraud events detected and time to resolve.

ideas.title: Exit Desk for Orphaned Local-Marketing Assets
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price service that finds, takes back and migrates the domain, listing, phone numbers and ad accounts locked inside shrinking legacy marketing vendors.
ideas.customer: Home-service and retail owners paying $200-1,200 a month to Yellow Pages descendants, marketing agencies and template-site hosts.
ideas.problem: Thryv's 2025 revenue was $785M and falling, with net income near $0.3M, so the vendor base is melting through price hikes, resales and shutdowns. Owners often do not own their domain, Google Business Profile admin rights, call-tracking numbers or ad accounts, and leaving means losing the phone number painted on the truck. Getting customers is still the top small-business challenge.
ideas.solution: A fixed-fee audit finds recurring vendor debits (via bank feed or bookkeeper), checks who owns each asset (WHOIS, GBP owner list, ad-account admin, tracking numbers), then executes the takeback: domain transfer, GBP ownership transfer, number port, site migration into an owner-owned stack, and contract cancellation notices. Optional monitoring alerts if a vendor re-takes control.
ideas.why_now: Legacy vendor decline is visible in public financials, AI site builders make replacement stacks cheap, and small businesses still need customers.
ideas.revenue_model: $299-799 one-time, $29/month monitoring, and referral fees from the destination stack (hosting, CRM, review tools).
ideas.non_obvious_insight: What the owner is paying for is a person who answers the phone, not leads. The exit is a control and trust problem more than a marketing problem. The bookkeeper sees the debit but has no workflow to end it.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with 10 bookkeepers to flag legacy-vendor debits. Run 20 audits and publish a 'who owns your phone number' checklist to seed leads.

ideas.title: Continuity Vault for Solo Operators
ideas.one_liner: A break-glass vault, dead-man switch and runbook so a solo business survives its owner's hospitalization or death, and its AI agents stop cleanly.
ideas.customer: Solo and two-person business owners aged 45+, reached through independent life-insurance agents, estate attorneys, SBA lenders and CPAs.
ideas.problem: For the majority of small businesses that are solo operations, the owner is the only person with access to the bank, domain, Google listing, payroll, customer list and payment processor. When the owner is incapacitated, nobody can legally or technically act. Delegated AI agents and OAuth tokens add new failure modes because they keep acting, or fail, without supervision.
ideas.solution: An encrypted vault with a named successor, dead-man switch, and pre-authorized runbook: the top ten bills, customer notification templates, who to call, how to pause automated agents and revoke tokens, and a wind-down-or-sell pack with a handoff to a route or book sale.
ideas.why_now: Owners increasingly hand credentials to AI agents and automations, and the 2026 loosening of SBA lending (7(a) plus 504 up to $10M) makes lenders care about key-person risk. The boomer owner cohort is aging.
ideas.revenue_model: $199 setup plus $19/month direct, wholesale at $99 per client to advisors, and API licensing to lenders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For the smallest businesses, succession usually means continuity, not sale. The distributor is the person who sells the life policy, who needs a reason to call every client each year.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit five independent insurance agents or estate attorneys and offer white-label onboarding for 50 clients. Test whether successors can complete a simulated break-glass drill in under an hour.

ideas.title: Lead-Refund Recovery for Home-Service Pros
ideas.one_liner: Auto-dispute junk paid leads from Google Local Services, Angi, Thumbtack and Yelp, and take a share of the credits recovered.
ideas.customer: HVAC, plumbing, roofing, locksmith, garage-door, pest and electrical firms with 3-30 employees spending $2k-30k a month on paid leads.
ideas.problem: A large share of paid leads are spam, wrong-service, out-of-area or duplicates (typically cited at 20-40%; prior knowledge). Disputes are manual and deadline-bound, so owners rarely file. Getting customers is the top small-business challenge, so the spend is untouchable but the waste is fixable.
ideas.solution: Connect ad and lead accounts and the phone system's call recordings. Transcribe and classify each lead against each platform's dispute reasons, file disputes with evidence inside the window, track credits, and flag chronically junky sources. A monthly report shows net cost per real lead.
ideas.why_now: Cheap call transcription and LLM classification make per-lead review nearly free, and legacy local-marketing vendors are shrinking and raising prices, which raises the value of every recovered credit.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-25% of credits recovered (no credit, no fee), or $99/month per account.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody sells lead-refund recovery because each dispute is worth $30-150, but automation turns them into a portfolio. Recovered credits are pure margin for the owner.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask 10 contractors from local trade Facebook groups for 90 days of lead exports and call logs. File disputes manually to learn acceptance rates, then automate the top three reason codes.

ideas.title: CAM and Insurance Pass-Through Audits for Micro-Tenants
ideas.one_liner: Read a small tenant's lease, recompute the landlord's annual reconciliation, and dispute overcharges inside the audit window, on contingency.
ideas.customer: Restaurants, salons, clinics, gyms and boutiques on NNN or modified-gross leases in strip centers and small retail, typically 1,000-5,000 sq ft.
ideas.problem: Landlord reconciliations of common-area, tax and insurance charges are opaque, and pass-throughs rose with property insurance and tax bills (prior knowledge). Audit rights exist in the lease but expire in weeks or months, and owners never read the lease. Rising costs are the top financial challenge for small firms.
ideas.solution: Upload the lease and reconciliation. An LLM extracts audit rights, caps, exclusions, gross-up, base year, admin fees and pro-rata share, recomputes the statement, drafts the audit request or dispute letter, calendars deadlines, and escalates to an auditor partner for contested items. Add a renewal-negotiation packet.
ideas.why_now: Long-context models read leases cheaply. Enterprise tenants have lease-audit firms, but micro-tenants were never worth the hourly rate.
ideas.revenue_model: 25-30% of amounts recovered, with a $99 flat triage fee for leases that show no error.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The lever is the deadline, not the arithmetic. Most owners have never seen their own audit clause, and landlords count on that.
ideas.first_30_days: Collect 10 leases and reconciliations through a restaurant association or business improvement district. Run manual audits, measure the hit rate, sign the first contingency deals and refine the extraction.

ideas.title: Notice Desk with Contingency Penalty Abatement
ideas.one_liner: Snap a photo of any IRS or state notice, get triage and a response, and pay only if the penalty is abated.
ideas.customer: 1-25 employee firms, S-corps and small partnerships that received late-filing, payroll-deposit, information-return mismatch or state tax notices.
ideas.problem: Notices sit in a drawer or a registered-agent inbox while penalties compound. Abatement routes (first-time abatement, reasonable cause, small-partnership relief) are well established but owners don't know them, and CPAs bill hourly. Filing rules are shifting: the 1099-NEC floor rose to $2,000, 1099-K thresholds reverted, and new tips and overtime reporting will create mismatches. IRS capacity appears strained (prior knowledge).
ideas.solution: Forward or photograph the notice. The system classifies it, extracts the deadline and amount, explains the options and drafts the response. An enrolled agent or CPA partner signs, files the abatement request and tracks it. State-notice variants are added by jurisdiction. A $19/month mail-monitoring plan for registered-agent customers catches new notices.
ideas.why_now: BOI filing services just lost their main product and need a new recurring hook, and compliance work is moving from filing to interpretation. LLMs can read notices at scale.
ideas.revenue_model: 20% of penalties abated, $49 flat for triage on notices with no abatement path, and $19/month monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A penalty notice is a lead with a known dollar value. Many abatements are near-automatic, so outcome pricing beats hourly billing, and Intuit, Xero and H&R Block cannot easily price on outcomes.
ideas.first_30_days: Get 100 anonymized notices from CPA partners and registered-agent companies to train the classifier. Sign an enrolled agent, run 30 abatements sourced from small-business forums, and record the abatement rate.

ideas.title: Certified SDE for Sub-$1M Business Sales
ideas.one_liner: A CPA-signed, AI-prepared earnings certificate that lets brokers, buyers and SBA lenders trust a small business's seller's discretionary earnings.
ideas.customer: Business brokers, SBA lenders and first-time buyers in $100k-$1M main-street deals, and the sellers who pay to be believed.
ideas.problem: A full quality-of-earnings review costs $15-50k, which is impossible on a $300k deal, so cash-heavy books and owner add-backs create distrust. Deals die in diligence or stall in lender underwriting. Search funds target $5-50M businesses and nothing standardizes trust for the smallest tier.
ideas.solution: Upload three years of returns, bank and processor statements and POS data. The system reconstructs revenue, recasts SDE with add-back evidence, and flags unrecorded revenue or personal expenses. A CPA signs a certified SDE range in 48 hours. Partner lenders accept the standard report, and it links to the escrow and route-sale flow.
ideas.why_now: SBA 7(a) plus 504 financing up to $10M began July 2026, so buyer demand and lender appetite are rising. LLMs and bank data make the reconstruction cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $495-995 per report paid by the seller or broker, lender licensing, and buyer diligence upsells.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: At this size the bottleneck is neither buyers nor capital but trust in the earnings number. A QoE costs 5% of price, and a cheap certificate unlocks the whole tier.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign three brokers who list $200k-800k deals and produce 15 reports manually with a CPA. Ask one SBA lender in writing what it needs in order to accept the certificate.

ideas.title: Drive-By Lawsuit Shield for Marketing Stacks
ideas.one_liner: Scan and fix the text, website and review flows that trigger serial-plaintiff demand letters, and back it with a response pack.
ideas.customer: Local-service SMBs and small multi-location brands, sold mostly through local marketing agencies and agency resellers on GoHighLevel, Wix and Squarespace.
ideas.problem: Serial-plaintiff waves target small firms: text-message consent and quiet-hours claims, website accessibility claims, wiretap claims over chat widgets and tracking pixels, and the FTC's fake-and-gated-review rule (prior knowledge on the rules). Demands of $5-25k get settled blind. AI-generated marketing raises exposure: 83% of AI-using small firms use AI for writing or marketing.
ideas.solution: A scanner checks known triggers: SMS consent capture and state quiet hours, trackers and chat widgets without consent banners, basic accessibility failures, review-gating flows and unsubstantiated claims. It applies or guides fixes, keeps a provenance-stamped consent ledger, and provides a demand-letter response pack via a partner law firm. Defense-cost coverage can be added through an MGA.
ideas.why_now: SMBs are now running automated texting, AI-written content and review requests, and small businesses lack legal capacity to evaluate demands.
ideas.revenue_model: $19-49 per site or number per month, $499 per response pack, plus a share of insurance premiums.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The vendor who sells the marketing tool never gets sued, but the owner does, and the agency is liable to its client. The buyer of protection is the agency reseller, not the owner.
ideas.first_30_days: Build scanners for three triggers and run free scans on 500 local sites. Sell reports to 10 agencies and sign a law-firm partner for the response pack.

ideas.title: Owner-Download: Capture Tacit Knowledge Before Sale
ideas.one_liner: Passively capture 60-90 days of an owner's calls, messages and jobs into a transferable playbook and a question-answering agent for the buyer.
ideas.customer: Owners aged 58+ of owner-dependent service and professional businesses ($300k-3M revenue) planning a sale in 12-36 months, plus the brokers who list them and the buyers who acquire them.
ideas.problem: Buyers discount hard for key-person dependency. The knowledge sits in the owner's head and phone: pricing instincts, customer quirks, vendor favors, unwritten rules. The traditional six-month handover rarely captures it.
ideas.solution: With consent, capture call recordings, texts and email, invoices, calendar and short weekly AI interviews. Produce SOPs, customer memory cards, learned pricing and quote logic, vendor scorecards and 'if X breaks, do Y' runbooks. The buyer gets a Q&A agent for year one ('how did the owner price gutters over 40 feet?') and the package goes in the data room as a transferable asset.
ideas.why_now: Long-context models, cheap call transcription and agentic retrieval make passive capture practical. Loosened SBA financing (up to $10M combined from July 2026) is drawing more first-time buyers who need this.
ideas.revenue_model: $2,500-6,000 per owner, broker referral fees, and a $199/month buyer subscription to the Q&A agent for 12 months.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: AI did not make this possible by automating the work but by making capture passive, so an owner no longer has to stop working to write manuals. Key-person discount is measurable, so the package can be priced against it.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit five owners through two brokers in one vertical (HVAC, plumbing or landscaping). Run the capture pilots and ask buyers to rate the packages against a control listing on confidence and price.

ideas.title: Agent-Bookable Gateway for Local Trades
ideas.one_liner: A per-business endpoint that lets consumers' AI agents get a photo-based quote, hold a slot and pay a deposit at a local trade without a phone call.
ideas.customer: House cleaners, junk-removal crews, pressure washers, mobile detailers, movers, handymen and groomers (1-15 staff) with weak or template websites.
ideas.problem: Consumers increasingly ask assistants to 'find and book' local help. Agents can't get a price, slot or deposit from a local trade without a call, so trades are invisible to agent-driven demand. Reviews and SEO matter less than being machine-readable and bookable.
ideas.solution: Each business gets an agent endpoint: photo-to-quote with vision models, service area and rules (minimum job, blackout dates), live slot holds, and a payment link for the deposit. It is exposed through structured data, an OpenAPI or MCP interface, and registered with agent platforms and directories. Owners set guardrails and approve borderline quotes by text.
ideas.why_now: Consumer agents and agentic-commerce protocols emerged in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), vision models can price photo-priceable jobs, and 46% of small firms already use AI, so owners are open to the concept.
ideas.revenue_model: $49/month plus a 3-5% booking fee on agent-originated jobs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The next website is a callable endpoint, and the first vertical where agents can close is the one where jobs are priceable from photos. Scheduling incumbents hold the data but may not expose a public agent interface, so a neutral gateway can win a directory position.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 20 operators in two photo-priceable verticals, publish their endpoints and test with the major assistants' agent modes plus manual concierge. Measure agent-originated bookings and quote accuracy.

ideas.title: Insured Filing Clerk for Multi-City Contractor Licenses
ideas.one_liner: A computer-use agent that renews and files contractor and business licenses across city and county portals that have no APIs, backed by a penalty warranty.
ideas.customer: Trade contractors (electricians, plumbers, HVAC, roofers, landscapers, painters), mobile groomers, food trucks and short-term-rental hosts working across many cities or counties, with 2-30 employees.
ideas.problem: Each city and county has its own business-license, registration and permit portal, fee schedule and renewal date, with COI and bond uploads. Missing one triggers fines or stop-work orders. Enterprise-priced compliance vendors ignore small firms, and payroll vendors are bundling only payroll compliance (Gusto bought Mosey in April 2026).
ideas.solution: An agent operates the same portals a human would to renew, upload COIs and bonds, pay fees with a virtual card and capture receipts. Human reviewers verify sensitive steps. A warranty pays penalties for missed or incorrect filings. Every filing improves a jurisdiction knowledge base of forms, fees and quirks.
ideas.why_now: Browser and computer-use agents crossed a reliability threshold in 2025-26, and payroll compliance has been productized, leaving licenses and permits as the untouched adjacent layer.
ideas.revenue_model: $59/month plus $15 per filing plus fee pass-through, with the warranty cost built into pricing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: With roughly 19,000 municipalities, no API strategy will ever cover the map, but an agent that uses the human interface can. The moat is the jurisdiction graph and the warranty.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick a dense metro cluster with many cities and one trade. Assist 20 contractors with renewals, recording each portal flow, and sign a COI and bond partner for bulk uploads. Track error rate and hours saved.

ideas.title: Weather-Indexed Revenue Cover for Outdoor Micro-Businesses
ideas.one_liner: Per-day parametric policies that pay out within an hour when rain, heat or smoke hits a vendor's venue, priced from the vendor's own sales history.
ideas.customer: Farmers-market vendors, food trucks, festival vendors, ice cream and shaved-ice stands, seasonal farm stands and outdoor fitness operators.
ideas.problem: A rain day or heat wave can erase a day's sales and cannot be insured through conventional policies. Margins are thin, and small owners (about 64% of nonemployers in trouble) fall back on personal funds.
ideas.solution: Micro-policies bought per market day or season. A fixed payout triggers when measured rainfall, temperature or air quality at the venue exceeds a threshold during the market window. Premium and payout are calibrated to each vendor's baseline sales from POS or bank data, and payment goes out over instant rails. Distribution goes through market associations and POS apps.
ideas.why_now: Instant payout rails, POS and bank APIs for baseline sales, cheap gridded weather data, and reinsurer interest in parametric small-business products make this feasible for a small MGA team.
ideas.revenue_model: MGA margin on premiums of about $6-15 per vendor-day, plus program fees from market associations.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is manageable when triggers are set per venue and per day, and the product is cash within an hour of the rain rather than indemnity after paperwork. Vendors will buy small daily coverage bundled into their booth fee.
