ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one market association (about 100 vendors) and an MGA or fronting carrier. Structure a season-long pilot under a master policy and price it from vendors' POS history. Track claims and basis risk.

ideas.title: Small-Claims Autopilot for Unpaid Invoices
ideas.one_liner: Take a solo operator from unpaid invoice to demand letter, filing, service, hearing prep and enforcement in a self-help flow.
ideas.customer: Freelancers, contractors and small B2B suppliers with $1k-20k unpaid invoices and no lawyer.
ideas.problem: Chasing fails, lawyers cost more than the claim, and small-claims procedure (forms, service, evidence, hearing, enforcement) is confusing, so most owners write off the debt. Cash is tight: nonemployers are less likely to be profitable and lean on personal funds.
ideas.solution: Connect invoices, email and texts. The system builds an evidence timeline, verifies the debtor entity and registered agent through state records, drafts a statutory-interest demand letter, files via e-filing where supported, schedules service, and prepares a hearing script and enforcement steps (garnishment and lien templates). It runs as a self-help tool, with a partner attorney for contested cases.
ideas.why_now: LLMs read messy invoice and message threads, e-filing is expanding in many courts, and nonemployer cash flow is under stress.
ideas.revenue_model: $79 flat per claim plus 10-15% of amounts collected, or a subscription for repeat filers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The demand letter itself resolves a large share of cases, and enforcement of the judgment is where the value sits, so the product should cover the full path. The regulatory edge is self-help positioning and attorney partners (the FTC's DoNotPay order shows the limits; prior knowledge).
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two states with online filing and $10k-plus limits. Run 30 claims for freelancers and trades sourced from community groups, and publish recovery rates and time to payment.

ideas.title: Surety Bonds for Agent Operators
ideas.one_liner: A customs bond for bots: agent operators post a surety-backed bond so sites, APIs and merchants can say yes to their agents and get paid if the agents misbehave.
ideas.customer: Mid-size vendors of browser, shopping and procurement agents ($1M-$50M ARR) whose agents get blocked or throttled. They pay for the bond and credential. Merchants and API providers consume the signal for free.
ideas.problem: Agent identity schemes (signed agents, know-your-agent) say who an agent is, not who pays when it scrapes abusively, mis-buys or triggers chargebacks. Agents are cheap to recreate, so identity carries no cost of failure. Bots are now 57.4% of requests, so sites default to blocking. After the August 2026 Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, blocking has to rest on contract and technical measures, so sites need a concrete reason to let agents in.
ideas.solution: Underwrite the operator (KYB, behavior review, volume caps). Issue a surety or insurer-backed bond ($25k-$1M penal sum) plus a signed credential that plugs into existing agent-auth headers and protocols. Sites whitelist a bonded lane with higher rate limits. A small claims desk pays on signed request logs. Wedge: agent vendors selling into mid-market merchants and B2B API providers that would create a bonded lane in their bot rules.
ideas.why_now: Bots overtook humans in 2026, and the Ninth Circuit ruling shifts blocking to contract terms. Neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding agent-dispute rule, and Visa's merchant dispute threshold tightened to 1.5% in April 2026, so merchants are risk-averse. Bonding has been proposed only in academic papers so far, and no product exists.
ideas.revenue_model: Bond premium share (typically 1-3% of penal sum per year) plus a $500-$5,000/month underwriting and credential fee, plus surety agency commission.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Trust that scales in commerce rests on bonds, not identity. Freight brokers, contractors and customs brokers all post bonds. A bond makes an operator's reputation costly to abandon, and a site only has to trust the surety, not the operator.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with a small surety agency or MGA to draft a miscellaneous bond form and a claims evidence standard. Recruit 5 agent vendors that merchants block and 5 merchants or API providers willing to whitelist. Sell the first 3 pilot bonds at $500-$1,500 per year plus a setup fee.

ideas.title: Agent-Access Terms Index for Enterprises
ideas.one_liner: A living database and alert feed of what the top 500 SaaS and data vendors allow, meter and prohibit when your AI agents touch their APIs and data.
ideas.customer: General counsel, procurement and IT platform leads at 100-5,000 employee companies deploying agents, plus their outside counsel. SaaS vendors are a later customer.
ideas.problem: Most insiders read the Ninth Circuit ruling (the user, not the agent vendor, accessed Amazon) as 'agents can roam free'. For enterprises it means the fight moves to contract, and the user's company is the bound party. Vendors are already moving. SAP restricts third-party AI agent access to its APIs, Slack has throttled non-Marketplace apps and banned persistent indexes, and ServiceNow throttles inbound agent traffic. Vendors are also adding agent-action meters. No one tracks any of this, so a company can breach terms at a dozen vendors and learn about it from a suspension or audit letter.
ideas.solution: Build a structured agent-use rights matrix for about 500 vendors: allowed, banned or priced, rate limits, indexing, retention and training clauses, and official connector alternatives. Add change detection on terms and API policy pages with plain-English diffs. Add a connector that maps your OAuth-connected apps and agent inventory to the matrix and flags conflicts. Include a clause library, negotiation playbooks and an audit-defense pack.
ideas.why_now: Platform lockdowns (SAP, Slack, ServiceNow) and per-agent-action pricing arrived in 2025-26, and the Ninth Circuit ruling (August 2026) made contract the main battleground. Amazon can still seek rehearing, which adds uncertainty buyers want tracked.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-5k/month subscriptions for legal and procurement teams, $8-25k fixed-fee exposure reviews and negotiation packages, and later vendor-side benchmarking.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Contract terms are becoming the price list and permission system of the agent economy, and they sit in unstructured legalese nobody indexes. The index is also the negotiating leverage, because it shows a buyer what comparable vendors concede.
ideas.first_30_days: Have an LLM plus a contract lawyer parse the terms and API policies of the top 100 SaaS vendors. Publish a free Agent Rights Scorecard for 25 of them to generate inbound. Sign 5 design partners at $1.5k/month and offer a $8-15k agent contract exposure review.

ideas.title: Flat-Fee Guarantee Against Runaway Agent Bills
ideas.one_liner: Pay a few percent on top of model spend and the guarantee absorbs any overnight blowout above a hard multiple of baseline, enforced by an inline kill switch.
ideas.customer: AI-native startups and agencies spending $5k-$200k per month on model and tool calls (seed to Series B), including dev shops deploying agents for clients.
ideas.problem: Retry loops turn $0.40 tasks into $40, and five-figure overnight bills are reported. Blended token prices fell about 67% in a year but agentic workflows burn 5-30x more tokens, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets. The market sells dashboards and caps. Nobody sells a promise, and founders and their investors want the tail risk gone.
ideas.solution: A drop-in proxy (change one base URL) that sees all model and tool traffic and learns a rolling baseline per agent and workflow. The guarantee covers spend above a set multiple of baseline in a rolling window (for example 4x over 6 hours), up to a cap, paid as cash or credits. The proxy enforces circuit breakers so maximum loss is bounded, which makes underwriting tractable. Coverage applies only where default breaker policies were accepted, which controls moral hazard.
ideas.why_now: TechCrunch was covering the scramble over runaway AI costs by June 2026. Gateways are being absorbed into security suites (Palo Alto bought Portkey), and dozens of cap-and-alert tools have commoditized enforcement without offering a guarantee.
ideas.revenue_model: 3-6% premium on metered spend plus a gateway subscription, with parametric or MGA reinsurance for large limits.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Whoever owns the kill switch can price the tail. A capped, enforced exposure is a parametric insurance product, not an open-ended liability. Buyers are paying for certainty, and the tooling is only how you deliver it.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible proxy with breakers. Sign 10 startups to a beta guarantee capped at about $2k per incident, backed by a roughly $20k reserve. Price at about 4% of spend and log every incident. Talk to two parametric or MGA capacity providers.

ideas.title: Revenue Recovery From Blocked Shopping Agents
ideas.one_liner: Synthetic agent shoppers try to buy from your store every night, find where bot defenses and checkout kill legitimate agent orders, and you pay a cut of the sales recovered.
ideas.customer: Mid-market e-commerce merchants ($5M-$200M GMV) on Shopify Plus, BigCommerce or Adobe Commerce with aggressive bot, WAF and fraud settings, reached through their agencies and fraud vendors.
ideas.problem: Insiders think the bottleneck is protocol adoption (ACP vs UCP vs AP2). The measurable leak is simpler. Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout. Fraud and bot systems built for humans misclassify agent traffic (Chargebacks911 warns of a false-decline problem). CAPTCHAs, SMS one-time codes and 3DS challenges kill legitimate agent orders, and the lost sale looks like a bounce, so no dashboard shows it.
ideas.solution: Run real agent stacks (ChatGPT agent mode, Comet, Gemini, open-source browser agents, plus ACP/UCP/AP2 clients) through scripted purchase journeys on the live store with test cards. Log the exact failure point: challenge page, WAF rule, OTP step, stale feed, price mismatch. Deliver a weekly fix list (allowlist verified agent signatures, rule changes, checkout patches), then re-test to prove recovery.
ideas.why_now: Bots now outnumber humans. Stores that blocked AI bots in 2024 are undoing it, and the Ninth Circuit ruling makes user-directed agents legitimate visitors. Five competing checkout protocols make failure modes hard to see.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k fixed audit plus 5-10% of attributable recovered agent revenue for 12 months, or $500-$2k/month monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A performance-fee audit is easy to buy because the merchant risks nothing. The proof is measurable (before and after test purchases), and the data becomes a benchmark of which defenses block which agents.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the harness with 3 agent stacks and 5 common checkout and WAF patterns. Offer 10 free audits to Shopify agencies who can resell. Convert the first 3 leaks worth over $5k per month into revenue-share contracts.

ideas.title: Valet Keys for Delegated Browser Sessions
ideas.one_liner: An enforcement layer that lets an agent act inside your logged-in bank, airline or supplier portal, but only within per-site limits such as read-only here and a spend cap there.
ideas.customer: Enterprise finance-ops, revenue-cycle and logistics teams running browser agents on portals with no API (20-500 seats), followed by builders of prosumer browser agents who need a safety story.
ideas.problem: Insiders are building agent identity (OAuth for agents), but most delegated work rides on cookies in sites with no API. The agent inherits the user's full session. Browsers offer no primitive for a user to see, scope or withdraw an agent's access. If the user is legally the one who accessed the site, as the Ninth Circuit reasoned, the user owns everything the agent does with that session.
ideas.solution: A browser extension plus enforcement proxy with per-site policy packs that classify actions (view, draft, submit, pay, change credentials) using URL, DOM and network patterns. Irreversible actions are denied by default, with spend and count caps, step-up approval and signed action receipts. Ship maintained packs for the top 200 enterprise portals (payer, carrier, marketplace seller-center and bank portals) and update them as sites change.
ideas.why_now: Browser agents went mainstream in 2026, and about 21,600 OpenClaw instances were found exposed. Machine identities outnumber humans roughly 109 to 1, and the agent-equals-user doctrine puts liability on the delegating user.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40 per seat per month for enterprises, policy-pack subscriptions, and a per-session API price for agent vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The missing primitive is a valet key (parks the car, cannot open the trunk) for sessions. The moat is the maintained per-site action taxonomy, which is tedious, unglamorous and hard to copy.
ideas.first_30_days: Find one revenue-cycle or logistics ops team already using browser agents and build read-only plus draft-only policy packs for the 5 portals they use. Run a $2k/month pilot and log blocked actions as proof of value.

ideas.title: Independent Audits for Per-Outcome Agent Invoices
ideas.one_liner: The DoubleVerify of AI agents: sample and verify the resolutions, meetings and approvals you were billed for, then claim credits for the fakes.
ideas.customer: Finance, procurement and support-ops leaders at companies paying $50k-$5M a year to outcome-priced agent vendors (support resolutions, AP processing, claims, scheduling).
ideas.problem: Vendors have moved from seats to outcomes. Reportedly, Zendesk narrowed billing to LLM-verified 'resolutions' at about $1.20-$1.50 each and HubSpot's customer agent charges about $0.50 per resolved conversation. The vendor defines and grades its own outcome, and buyers cannot tell a real resolution from a customer who gave up. Step two of falling token prices is vendors with an incentive to over-count outcomes.
ideas.solution: A read-only connector to the buyer's helpdesk, CRM or ERP that re-derives outcomes independently from reopen rates, repeat contacts in 7-14 days, silent abandonment, escalation to humans and sentiment. Sample about 300 outcomes a month for blind human plus LLM review. Deliver a monthly invoice integrity report with the false-outcome rate and a credit-claim packet aligned to the contract's dispute window.
ideas.why_now: Outcome pricing became mainstream in 2026, and Deloitte published guidance in June 2026 on accounting for it, which signals CFO attention. Buyers paying per outcome have no independent measurement.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-20% of credits recovered plus a $2-6k/month subscription. The buy side pays first to avoid conflict, and vendors may later pay for an audited badge.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Ad tech showed that when sellers measure their own outcomes, a third-party verifier becomes a category (DoubleVerify, IAS). Agent outcome pricing recreates that conflict with almost no independent measurement, and the earliest data is anonymous benchmarks of false-resolution rates.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 companies using Fin, Zendesk or HubSpot agents through support-ops communities. Run a free or contingency retrospective audit of 3 months of invoices and publish anonymized false-resolution rates to seed demand.

ideas.title: Legal Hold and Discovery for Agent Traces
ideas.one_liner: Custodian mapping, hold notices and defensible export for the agent logs that are becoming the new email in litigation.
ideas.customer: Litigation-support teams at mid-size law firms and corporate legal-ops or GC teams at companies running agents, with boutique e-discovery providers as a channel.
ideas.problem: Agent traces (prompts, tool calls, retrievals, memory) sit in observability tools and vendor consoles with retention defaults of days to weeks. They are not on custodian charts, and at least one court has treated AI-generated content as discoverable, exposing parties to Rule 37(e) spoliation sanctions. EDRM and law-firm alerts in mid-2026 say agent logs become evidence when agents fail, but nobody sells the plumbing.
ideas.solution: Connectors to Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry and S3 stores, agent platform APIs and cloud logs. They inventory where traces live, generate agent custodian maps, flag legal holds and suspend deletion where APIs allow, snapshot with hash chains, redact PII and privileged material, and export to Relativity, Everlaw or Reveal. Add hold-aware deletion to reconcile GDPR erasure requests with active holds, and a Rule 26(f) checklist.
ideas.why_now: Agents moved into production across 2026, and the discovery literature has just started addressing agent traces. Observability vendors optimized for developer debugging (short retention, cheap storage), which is the opposite of what litigation needs.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-10k per matter plus $1-3k/month per connected source, with revenue share for e-discovery channel partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: E-discovery vendors will need new data sources the way they needed Slack and Teams connectors. Whoever owns the connectors to agent trace stores becomes the toll gate, and forensics tools that reconstruct incidents are not litigation-grade preservation.
ideas.first_30_days: Build 3 connectors (Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry/S3) and a one-page hold notice and agent custodian questionnaire. Recruit 3 boutique litigation-support firms as pilots and sell a $5k agent ESI readiness assessment to GCs.

ideas.title: Estate Planning for People's AI Agents
ideas.one_liner: Powers of attorney, dead-man switches and revocation tooling for the agents that hold standing authority over your money, email and subscriptions.
ideas.customer: Estate-planning attorneys and RIAs or family offices serving tech founders and executives who already run personal agents, followed by consumers through those channels.
ideas.problem: Personal agents now hold standing authority: card mandates, wallets, email access, autopay and negotiations. Step two: authority is tied to a living principal. Step three: death, incapacity, divorce or bankruptcy leaves agents acting on stale instructions or locks heirs out. Fiduciary access laws (for example RUFADAA) give no automatic access to digital accounts, and nobody has drafted for delegated software.
ideas.solution: An Agent Schedule for estate plans. It combines an inventory of agents, OAuth grants, wallets and mandates (via connectors), attorney-drafted clauses giving a digital fiduciary authority to pause, transfer or delete agents and limiting post-death actions, an incapacity or dead-man trigger that rotates credentials and downgrades permissions to read-only while notifying the fiduciary, and export of agent memory and logs for the executor.
ideas.why_now: Personal agents went mainstream in 2026 (OpenClaw reached about 247k GitHub stars), and agentic wallets and machine-payment rails launched in February and March 2026. The estate bar is only starting to publish AI afterlife primers, and they focus on AI personas, not delegated agents.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-$1,500 per client schedule sold through attorneys (roughly $300 wholesale), $10-$30/month monitoring, and $5k/year RIA channel licenses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every technology that received delegated authority (checks, credit cards, cloud accounts) eventually got a legal instrument for the case where the principal stops existing. Agents have none yet, and the trigger events are guaranteed, so demand arrives on a calendar.
ideas.first_30_days: Draft the template with 2 estate attorneys. Pilot with 10 founders through an existing network. Build a simple inventory and revocation checklist using OAuth grant discovery for Google, Microsoft 365, GitHub and 5 agent platforms, and charge $750 per pilot.

ideas.title: Refundable Deposits Against AI Submission Floods
ideas.one_liner: A gateway that makes AI-generated reports, applications and pitches post a small refundable stake, so maintainers only read submissions someone bet on.
ideas.customer: Open-source maintainers and foundations, bug-bounty program owners, and other inboxes overwhelmed by AI-generated submissions (journals, grant makers, VC and press inboxes, public-comment portals). Start with OSS security teams and mid-size bounty programs.
ideas.problem: curl scrapped its bug bounty in January 2026 after valid reports fell below 5%, and its maintainer floated an entrance fee. HackerOne reportedly paused its Internet Bug Bounty in March after a 76% year-on-year jump in submissions, and other projects have retired bounties. Agents removed the effort-based backpressure open-source governance relied on. Content classifiers lose the arms race to models that write plausible reports.
ideas.solution: A stake API and form: the submitter (human or agent) posts a refundable deposit of $5-$50 by card or machine payment. Triage marks the report valid (refund plus any bounty) or invalid (deposit goes to maintainers or charity). Integrations for GitHub Security Advisories, email intake and bounty-platform webhooks. Reporters with track records get deposit discounts, and unpaid stakes flow to the program.
ideas.why_now: The curl and HackerOne events are recent and public. Machine Payments Protocol (March 2026) and card rails make small, programmatic deposits practical, and agents now file at scale.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-15% of forfeited deposits plus $99-$499/month per program for triage tooling, with sponsor-funded tiers for open-source projects.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Price is the only filter that scales with attacker capacity. An agent must risk money on every claim, honest reporters get refunded, so the cost lands only on slop. Postage as a spam filter failed when senders were humans, but agent-operated senders have budgets and ROI math.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a GitHub Security Advisory plus web-form integration in two weeks. Recruit 5 OSS projects that have publicly complained and run a 30-day pilot measuring valid-report rate. Then approach bounty platforms with the data.

ideas.title: Phishing Simulations for Agent Approvers
ideas.one_liner: Plant known-bad agent actions into human approval queues and prove to auditors and insurers that your reviewers actually catch them.
ideas.customer: Heads of finance ops, claims, compliance and internal audit at companies whose agents require human approval (payments, refunds, claims, access requests, code merges), plus cyber underwriters who ask about controls.
ideas.problem: Human-in-the-loop is the default answer to agent risk. Step two: volume makes approval a reflex, so the gate decays into a rubber stamp. Step three: regulators and auditors ask for oversight that is demonstrable and measurable (EU AI Act Article 14 and NIST AI RMF language), and no company can show that reviewers catch anything. Injected test cases are recommended in practice writing, but nobody productizes them.
ideas.solution: Middleware in the approval path (Slack, Teams, ServiceNow or custom queues) that injects synthetic, internally labeled bad cases at calibrated rates: a vendor bank-detail change, an out-of-policy refund, a prompt-injected request. It measures catch rate and latency by reviewer, queue and time of day, and adapts injection frequency. Output is an oversight effectiveness report with confidence intervals for auditors and insurers, plus queue-design advice (fewer, better gates).
ideas.why_now: Agents multiply approval volume. The EU AI Act's human-oversight requirements are still on the books for 2027 and insurers now ask about controls in questionnaires. Approval fatigue is widely acknowledged but unmeasured.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-8k/month per approval workflow, or $30-$100k/year enterprise licenses, with an audit-evidence add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: KnowBe4 built a large company by testing humans rather than training them. The presence of a reviewer is not a control, but a measured catch rate is, and it doubles as evidence in insurance and audit conversations.
ideas.first_30_days: Build for Slack approvals with an accounts-payable bank-change scenario. Run it with 3 finance-ops teams and deliver a first report stating how many planted errors reviewers caught. Use anonymized catch-rate results as the sales asset.

ideas.title: Managed Migrations When Models Get Retired
ideas.one_liner: We replay your agent's real traces on the replacement model, fix the regressions, and hand back a patched prompt and tool config with a pass/fail report before the deprecation date.
ideas.customer: Series A-C SaaS companies and enterprise automation teams running 1-20 production agents without a dedicated eval or ML team.
ideas.problem: Model versions are retired on schedules set by others (for example GitHub scheduled the removal of several Claude and Gemini versions in Copilot on 2026-09-01). When an agent is repointed to a newer model it keeps returning success codes while tool-call formatting, JSON adherence, refusal boundaries and token use silently change. Teams without eval infrastructure find out from customers.
ideas.solution: Fixed-fee migration sprints: capture golden traces, build assertions from tool traces, schemas and business rules, run baseline versus candidate models, tune prompts and tool descriptions, and report accuracy, latency and cost. A subscription Sunset Watch tracks about 20 providers' deprecation calendars and opens migration tickets automatically, with a self-serve replay tool later.
ideas.why_now: Retirement cadence accelerated across 2025-26, agents with multi-step tool use are more fragile than chat apps, and falling token prices tempt teams to switch models constantly.
ideas.revenue_model: $8-$25k per migration sprint and $1-3k/month for Sunset Watch.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The customers who most need migration cannot afford an eval team, which is why Y2K, Java and Windows migrations became services businesses. Deprecation calendars are set by providers, so demand is scheduled and forecastable.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish a public deprecation calendar and migration-risk checklist. Cold-offer sprints to 30 companies visibly on soon-to-be-retired models (found via job posts and public integrations). Do 2 discounted pilots.

ideas.title: Real Gross Margin Diligence for AI Startups
ideas.one_liner: Quality-of-earnings for agent companies: restate COGS at unsubsidized token prices, retry waste and expiring credits so investors see true unit economics.
ideas.customer: Growth-equity, PE and VC diligence teams and corporate M&A groups acquiring AI-native companies ($20M-$500M deals), and startups preparing a raise.
ideas.problem: Reported AI gross margins are flattered by free cloud and model credits, introductory rates and uncosted retries. Practitioners say diligence restates credits at renewal prices, and AI-native margins run around 50-60% versus 75-85% for classic SaaS. Agentic tasks use 5-30x more tokens, so cohort economics move fast. M&A is heating up (Okta bought Permiso for about $200M in July 2026, and Palo Alto bought Portkey and Koi). Traditional QoE firms lack telemetry fluency.
ideas.solution: Read-only connectors to billing exports, gateways, cloud invoices and product analytics. Produce cohort-level unsubsidized COGS per seat or outcome, sensitivity to price cuts and model swaps, tokens per customer growth, cost of failed runs and retries, and scaling curves. Five-day turnaround report, plus quarterly monitoring for fund portfolios.
ideas.why_now: An AI M&A wave and investors pricing trajectory over current margin. Credit-inflated margins matter more as promotional pricing expires, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-$40k per diligence engagement and $3-$8k/month portfolio monitoring subscriptions for funds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The margin story is hidden in gateway and billing logs, not the general ledger. Buyers pay a premium to avoid overpaying for subsidized revenue, and every engagement builds a private benchmark of credit-adjusted margins.
ideas.first_30_days: Write the data-request list and report template. Pitch 20 growth-stage funds and deal associates, deliver 2 discounted diligence reports, and publish an anonymized credit-adjusted gross margin benchmark to generate inbound.

ideas.title: SOX Evidence Packs for Agent-Run Controls
ideas.one_liner: Control libraries, walkthrough scripts and test evidence that let auditors accept AI agents inside financial close, AP and reconciliations.
ideas.customer: Controllers, SOX program managers and internal audit at US public companies ($500M-$10B revenue) piloting agents in finance, plus mid-tier audit firms that must test them.
ideas.problem: As of mid-2026 the PCAOB has no AI-specific standard. Auditors ask how agent actions are authorized, logged and reviewed, and whether agent-generated walkthroughs count as sufficient evidence. FEI's Committee on Corporate Reporting published an AI-in-ICFR framework in June 2026, but finance teams have no packaged controls or evidence format.
ideas.solution: A library of agent-specific controls mapped to COSO 2013 (access, prompt and model change management, completeness, override monitoring), with test scripts, sampling templates and an evidence collector that exports action logs, approval trails and change tickets in auditor-ready format. Start with a pre-interim readiness assessment.
ideas.why_now: Calendar-2026 audits are entering interim testing, the June 2026 FEI framework gives a hook, and a standards vacuum means the first accepted evidence format wins.
ideas.revenue_model: $20-$60k readiness assessments, $3-$8k/month evidence subscriptions, and license deals with audit firms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a standards vacuum, the first packaged evidence format an audit firm accepts becomes the de facto standard, as SOC 2 report formats did for cloud. Auditors are also under pressure to have an answer.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 2 former Big-4 SOX auditors and write 25 agent controls. Run free readiness workshops for 10 controllers already piloting agents in AP or close, and convert 2-3 to paid assessments.

ideas.title: Convert Legacy RPA Bots Using Their Own Logs
ideas.one_liner: Use years of bot execution logs as free ground-truth tests to convert brittle RPA bots into monitored agents at a fixed price per bot.
ideas.customer: Mid-market companies (500-10,000 employees) with 20-300 UiPath, Blue Prism or Power Automate bots in finance ops, claims and HR, plus RPA consultancies as a channel.
ideas.problem: Vendor and consultancy estimates put RPA upkeep at several times license cost, and UI changes break bots constantly. Leaders want agents but fear regression, and migration advice is generic ('retire the brittle ones first'). RPA vendors are pivoting to agentic pitches themselves, which increases pressure without giving a safe method.
ideas.solution: Ingest bot definitions and run logs, replay historical inputs to a candidate agent, and differentially test its outputs against the bot's recorded outputs. Cut over each bot when parity passes a threshold, keep the old bot in shadow for 30 days, monitor for drift, and price per bot converted plus a run-and-monitor fee.
ideas.why_now: Computer-use agents can operate UIs reliably enough to compete with scripted bots, and RPA vendors are moving to orchestration. Budgets are earmarked because maintenance costs are visible.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-$6k per bot conversion plus $200-$500/month per bot run and monitoring, with revenue share for consultancy partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The hard part of migrating automations is knowing the new one is right. Legacy bots have already produced years of labeled input-output pairs for free, which turns migration into differential testing.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 10 mid-market RPA shops and ask each for 5 brittle bots. Convert 5 bots across 2 customers in shadow mode, show parity, and sign a fixed-fee conversion for the next 20.

ideas.title: Pooled Guaranteed Throughput for Agent Builders
ideas.one_liner: Mid-market agent builders cannot meet reserved-capacity minimums, so we pool dozens of them into one commitment and sell guaranteed tokens-per-minute with failover.
ideas.customer: Agent-heavy SaaS companies and enterprise platform teams with $20k-$300k/month in model spend that hit rate limits and latency spikes at burst but cannot fill provisioned-throughput commitments.
ideas.problem: One agent task fans out into dozens of model and tool calls, multiplying request volume 10-50x. Provider tokens-per-minute ceilings and noisy neighbors cause 429s and latency spikes exactly when workflows burst. Reserved throughput exists but is sized for peak and billed monthly, so a mid-market buyer pays for capacity idle most of the day.
ideas.solution: A CSP-style aggregator and gateway that buys committed capacity across 2-3 providers, statistically multiplexes customers whose peaks do not coincide, and sells guaranteed-TPM slices with consolidated billing, per-tenant quotas and automatic cross-provider failover. Begin as a failover gateway, then graduate to pooled commitments once demand data proves the multiplexing gain.
ideas.why_now: Token prices fell about 67% in a year while agentic usage per task rose 5-30x, so capacity, not unit price, binds at peak. The gateway and sandbox layers are commoditizing (identical sandbox pricing), leaving supply-side pooling as a differentiator.
ideas.revenue_model: 10-20% spread on committed spend plus a platform fee for guaranteed-capacity tiers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as price, but for agents the binding constraint is burst capacity when a workflow fans out. Burstiness is diversifiable, like classic insurance pooling, and small buyers cannot pool on their own.
ideas.first_30_days: Launch a failover gateway with consolidated billing across Bedrock, Vertex and Azure (no commitment). Sign 10 design partners and collect hourly usage data, model the multiplexing gain, and negotiate the first pooled commitment with letters of intent in hand.

ideas.title: Pooled Buyer Mandates for Group Discounts
ideas.one_liner: Thousands of buyer agents sign standing purchase mandates ('I will pay up to $X if 200 others join') and vendors bid to fill the pooled demand.
ideas.customer: Startups and SMBs (10-200 employees) buying SaaS and business services (renewals, business insurance, telecom). Buyers pay a success fee and vendors pay for pre-committed demand.
ideas.problem: Small buyers lack bargaining power and time, and group purchasing organizations serve hospitals and enterprises, not the long tail. Vendors offer volume discounts against committed volume they cannot see. Agent payment standards now include signed intent mandates (Google's AP2, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent) that capture limits and constraints, and AP2 explicitly anticipates group scenarios, yet no product pools them.
ideas.solution: A mandate pool where each buyer or their agent signs an intent mandate with price ceiling, term and threshold. The exchange aggregates by category, shows vendors a live demand curve with reservation prices, and runs a sealed-bid reverse auction when the threshold is met. Purchases execute through each buyer's own payment mandate. First category: annual SaaS renewals, a Vendr for the long tail.
ideas.why_now: AP2 (September 2025), Verifiable Intent and UCP provide the first standard way to hold cryptographically signed, pre-authorized purchase intent. Agents now run procurement tasks, and vendors moving to agent meters want volume signals.
ideas.revenue_model: 5-10% of buyer savings or a 2-4% vendor fee on pooled transactions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A signed intent is a binding, machine-readable limit order for goods, so small buyers can pre-commit credibly without a human negotiating. That credibility is what makes group buying scale, like Kickstarter for procurement.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 100 startups from a founder community to pledge to 5 popular tools through a web form (protocol integration later). Bring the demand curve to 5 vendors and close one pooled deal to prove price.

ideas.title: Front Door for AI Callers at Local Businesses
ideas.one_liner: A phone-number layer that recognizes when the caller is an AI agent, answers instantly with pre-authorized quotes and availability, and routes real customers to humans.
ideas.customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (salons, groomers, HVAC and plumbing, auto shops, cleaners) with 1-20 staff, reached via marketing agencies and booking or field-service platforms. AI receptionist vendors are later licensees.
ideas.problem: Google's 'Have AI check pricing' agentic calling has rolled out to US Search users and expanded to home services in summer 2026. Businesses now get AI callers that tie up staff and harvest prices, and owners cannot tell agents from customers. In Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace simulation, buyer agents heavily favored the first proposal they received, so fast structured answers win business.
ideas.solution: Answer with an agent detector and an agent lane. If the caller identifies as or behaves like an AI (or presents a signed handshake), reply with a spoken and machine-readable quote from the owner's rate card and calendar within owner-set bounds, and log the outcome. Real customers go to humans. Publish a URL or DTMF handshake so compliant agents can switch from speech to structured data, the Gibberlink idea done with production-grade channels. Analytics show which agents call and quote win rates.
ideas.why_now: Agentic calling is live at Google scale, AI receptionists are common, and the 2025 Gibberlink demo proved the handshake idea but remains a proof of concept. Production agent protocols (MCP, A2A) do not cover phone calls to small businesses.
ideas.revenue_model: $49-$149/month per location, agency white-label deals, and later per-verified-handshake fees from agent platforms.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The phone is the API of the local economy and both ends are becoming machines that still talk in speech. Whoever owns the switch-to-data handshake and the seller's rate-card truth owns local agent commerce, and speed to first quote may matter more than price.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the call flow on a telephony API. Recruit 20 salons, groomers and HVAC shops through 3 local marketing agencies, log the AI calls they receive (many owners are unaware), and show AI calls answered and quotes won. Charge $79/month.

ideas.title: A Price Index and Exchange for Agent Labor
ideas.one_liner: Publish the going rate and accuracy for standardized agent-delivered tasks (per 1,000 invoices, per verified ticket resolution), then let buyers run reverse auctions against it.
ideas.customer: CFOs, procurement and ops leaders at enterprises buying agent services, investors and analysts, and later the agent vendors that bid for work.
ideas.problem: Buyers have no reference price. Vendor pricing is opaque and shifting from seats to outcomes, quality varies widely, and Gartner says only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic' vendors are real. Unit token prices fell about 67% but bills rose, so nobody knows what a task should cost.
ideas.solution: Define standardized task classes with public test sets and acceptance criteria (invoice extraction and coding, tier-1 support resolution, KYC document review, meeting scheduling). Run blinded monthly bake-offs across vendors on hidden holdouts and publish a quality and cost-per-verified-outcome index. Sell buyer-side bake-offs on customers' own data. Later add an RFQ exchange with escrow released when acceptance tests pass.
ideas.why_now: Outcome pricing arrived in 2026, agent-washing is rampant, and benchmarks exist for models but not end-to-end vendors. Project Vend-style real-world evaluations show that outcomes need checklists and supervision to be trustworthy.
ideas.revenue_model: $20-$60k/year subscriptions for enterprises and investors, $15-$40k custom bake-offs, and a 3-5% exchange take rate later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Markets need a benchmark price before they need a marketplace, as freight and housing indices came first. Agent labor has large quality and price dispersion, and the party that publishes the reference sets the negotiation frame for the whole category.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 2 task classes and assemble public plus holdout data. Run 6 vendors and publish the first index free with full methodology. Sell the first custom bake-off to a buyer and use it as a case study.

ideas.title: Signed Authority Certificates for Buying Agents
ideas.one_liner: Companies issue legally strong, machine-verifiable certificates saying which agent may order what, up to what amount, from whom, so suppliers can trust agent-placed orders.
ideas.customer: EU industrial distributors and wholesalers that receive purchase orders by email or EDI, and their larger business customers deploying procurement agents. Start with DACH and Benelux distributors.
ideas.problem: A supplier gets an order from 'Acme's purchasing agent' and has no way to know it may bind Acme to a EUR 50k purchase. AI makes fake purchase orders and business email compromise cheaper. Consumer-oriented agent-payment mandates (AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent) do not cover B2B signing authority, and research notes from 2026 say agents do not map cleanly onto EU digital wallet categories.
ideas.solution: An authority registry and issuance service. A company's legal representative signs a delegation certificate (qualified electronic signature via eIDAS trust providers, EUDI wallet later) covering agent key, scope (categories or SKUs), per-order and monthly limits, validity and revocation. Suppliers verify by API in under 200 ms and see remaining limit. Integrate with ERP order intake and e-invoicing. The signed record is court-grade evidence in disputes.
ideas.why_now: EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by end-2026, financial institutions are expected to accept them by December 2027, and qualified signatures already carry the legal effect of handwritten ones. Agent mandate standards exist but are consumer-centric.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 99-499/month per issuing company, EUR 0.05-0.20 per supplier verification, and enterprise licenses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Legal effect, not cryptography, is the scarce ingredient in B2B agent commerce. The EU uniquely has an instrument (the qualified signature) that turns a delegation into evidence courts accept, so build where the law already does the hard part.
ideas.first_30_days: Integrate with one qualified trust service provider for signing. Interview 20 distributors about agent-placed orders and PO fraud, pilot with 3 distributors and their top buyers on existing order intake, and collect letters of intent.

ideas.title: Wind Tunnel for Agent Markets and Pricing Collusion
ideas.one_liner: Simulate your pricing or buying agent against thousands of rival agents to see whether it drifts into tacit collusion, manipulation or first-offer traps before regulators or rivals do.
ideas.customer: Revenue-management and pricing-software vendors (hotels, multifamily, retail, insurance), marketplaces running agent-facing APIs, and the antitrust and compliance counsel who advise them. Regulators are a later customer.
ideas.problem: Academic work shows LLM pricing agents can converge on supracompetitive prices without communicating. Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace found agent buyers show strong first-proposal bias (a 10-30x advantage for response speed) and can be manipulated. Algorithmic pricing is already drawing antitrust suits and state laws, and nobody has a standard way to show a deployed pricing agent behaves competitively.
ideas.solution: Adapt the open-source Magentic Marketplace environment into a test harness with calibrated rival populations (LLM and RL agents). Run repeated-game tests measuring markups against a competitive baseline, information-leakage tests, and manipulation and first-offer sensitivity. Deliver an algorithmic pricing conduct report plus guardrails (randomization, no shared non-public data, price-parity limits) and re-test when the underlying model changes.
ideas.why_now: Agentic repricing is spreading, algorithmic-pricing enforcement is active, the simulation environment was open-sourced in late 2025, and models change every quarter so one-off audits go stale.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-$150k per audit, $5-$15k/month re-test subscriptions, and law-firm seat licenses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: You cannot inspect intent inside a model, but you can test behavior in a sandbox economy. Like crash tests for cars, a standardized, reproducible test gives defendants a documented duty-of-care defense and gives regulators a common yardstick.
ideas.first_30_days: Adapt Magentic Marketplace to a hospitality-pricing scenario and write a methodology note. Approach 3 antitrust boutiques and 3 revenue-management vendors, and sell a $25k pilot audit.

ideas.title: Bring-Into-Use Satellites for Spectrum Filing Holders
ideas.one_liner: Fixed-price rideshare satellites that let holders of valuable spectrum and orbit filings meet ITU hardware milestones instead of losing them.
ideas.customer: Telecom ministries and regulators of small and mid-size states (Gulf, Africa, Pacific, Central Asia, Latin America), plus startups that hold NGSO filings but cannot afford a full constellation.
ideas.problem: Spectrum and orbit rights are now priced like beachfront (EchoStar's reported $23B sale to AT&T and $17B sale to SpaceX), yet ITU rules still require real hardware in orbit by set deadlines. A holder of paper filings is one missed milestone from losing the asset, and a real constellation costs hundreds of millions.
ideas.solution: A standard 6U-12U bus with a software-defined payload configurable to the filed bands, sold as a 'milestone in a box'. The package covers rideshare launch, operations, evidence for the administration and coordination paperwork. Regulatory counsel decides what counts as bringing into use for each filing. Entry product is a filing-health audit built from public ITU data.
ideas.why_now: The 2025-26 EchoStar deals reset what spectrum is worth. Rideshare is plentiful (321 orbital launches in 2025 per the briefing). Commercial 6U buses and SDR payloads are off the shelf, and nine-figure rounds at European bus makers show integration capacity is growing. Sovereign space programs are multiplying.
ideas.revenue_model: Audit $20-50k. Fixed-price milestone satellite $1.5-4M. Annual retainer of $100-300k for filing maintenance and coordination. Optional success fee when a preserved filing is sold or leased.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat filings as paper assets and hardware as optional. The ITU makes hardware the price of keeping the paper, so the scarce thing is cheap, compliant placeholder hardware plus the regulatory playbook. Nobody sells that as a product.
ideas.first_30_days: Hire one ex-administration or ITU filing specialist on contract. Scrape public ITU filing data and rank about 100 filings by deadline urgency. Send personalized audits to 50 administrations and startups, and charge for the first five. Collect LOI-backed pre-orders before committing to hardware.

ideas.title: Used-Satellite Exchange With Independent Health Reports
ideas.one_liner: A broker and due-diligence shop that turns dead or distressed operators' on-orbit assets into sellable, verified inventory.
ideas.customer: Buyers: acquirers of the Rocket Lab type, infrastructure and PE funds, and governments or startups that want a quick constellation. Sellers: bankruptcy trustees, venture-debt lenders, insurers and cash-strapped first-generation smallsat operators.
ideas.problem: Insiders assume a satellite is worthless when its company dies. But the bus, license, orbit and customer contracts can still hold value, and buyers cannot verify condition. Lenders have no repossession or title process, and every M&A team improvises technical diligence.
ideas.solution: Two products. (1) An independent 'fleet health report' built from open orbital data (maneuver history, decay, propulsion-use proxies, beacon and telemetry checks) plus data-room review. (2) A brokerage that matches on-orbit assets and licenses to buyers, with regulator-approved license transfers handled by counsel.
ideas.why_now: Rocket Lab's roughly $8B Iridium deal and its CFO's 'more M&A' comment show on-orbit assets are being priced. 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025 means a large aging first-generation cohort. Funding is bifurcating into nine-figure rounds for a few winners and starvation for the rest.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-100k per health report. 3-8% success fee on brokered deals. Annual subscription for lenders and insurers who want portfolio monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In space, value sits in the license, the orbit and the operating bus, and none of the three dies with the company. The missing piece is trusted third-party verification, which is a service business rather than a rocket business.
ideas.first_30_days: Publish free health scorecards on 20 public constellations to build credibility. Interview five venture-debt lenders and two space insurers about their current diligence. Sell two paid reports to funds looking at consolidation targets. Ask trustees of failed smallsat companies to list assets with you.

ideas.title: SLA-Backed Mirror of At-Risk Public Earth Data
ideas.one_liner: A paid continuity service that keeps free federal Earth-observation feeds flowing, with bridge products and an SLA, when the originals degrade or go dark.
ideas.customer: Crop and weather insurers, commodity and energy trading desks, hydropower and utilities, and reinsurers whose models ingest free NOAA, NASA and USGS satellite products.
ideas.problem: Free satellite and climate feeds have no SLA. Since 2025, reported budget pressure and retirements (DMSP-derived products, some NOAA archives) and aging flagship sensors (MODIS-era platforms nearing end of life) have exposed downstream firms to a single point of failure they never underwrote.
ideas.solution: A 'Data Continuity Desk': mirror the top 50 at-risk feeds, cross-calibrate substitutes (VIIRS, Sentinel-3, Landsat, commercial sensors) into documented bridge products, alert on schema and quality changes, and contractually guarantee delivery. Add an audit that maps each customer's model to its data dependencies.
ideas.why_now: The briefing notes NOAA and NASA EO budget cuts were not covered, so treat specifics as unverified. Prior knowledge points to 2025-26 funding fights and curtailed products. Meanwhile Sentinel and commercial sensors are mature enough to serve as bridges.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-50k per year per data product under SLA. $15-40k for a dependency audit. Enterprise bundles for insurers and trading desks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders think free public data is a permanent public good. The businesses built on it hold an uninsured operational risk, and the seller who quantifies that risk and guarantees continuity gets paid like an insurer.
ideas.first_30_days: Inventory the 100 most cited NOAA, NASA and USGS feeds and score each for discontinuation risk. Publish the list, then call 30 insurers and trading desks and ask which feeds they run on. Build one bridge product, for example a snow or vegetation index, and sign two paid pilots.

ideas.title: Satellite Cannibalization Scores for Rural ISP Lenders
ideas.one_liner: Address-level risk scores that show which rural ISP portfolios LEO broadband will hollow out, and which it will not.
ideas.customer: Lenders to rural ISPs (cooperative and agricultural lenders, community banks), funds buying wireless or fiber ISPs, tower and fixed-wireless investors, and state broadband offices that allocate subsidies.
ideas.problem: Starlink went from 8.9M to 12M subscribers in six months (per the briefing) while ARPU fell 19% in one quarter. That means it is pricing down into the rural segments small ISPs live on. Lenders still underwrite these ISPs on legacy subscriber-count assumptions, and nobody can tell which locations are actually exposed.
ideas.solution: A data product that scores every serviceable location: fiber or cable alternatives, fixed wireless, LEO availability and price, local congestion, and expected churn or ARPU pressure. It rolls up to portfolio covenants, valuation adjustments and acquisition due-diligence reports. Updated monthly as satellite pricing and capacity change.
ideas.why_now: Subscriber growth of about 35% in six months, falling ARPU and satellite eligibility in subsidy programs all landed in 2025-26. Starship-driven capacity growth should push prices down further.
ideas.revenue_model: Portfolio subscription $2-10k per month per lender. $10-40k per acquisition due-diligence report. Data licensing to ISP-focused funds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The consensus is fiber wins and satellites lose. The actual exposure is mid-density fixed-wireless and DSL footprints, and the difference is visible at address level. Lenders get paid for knowing which side of that line each loan sits on.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a prototype on public availability maps, FCC broadband data and published Starlink plan tiers for three states. Pitch five agricultural or community lenders with a free look at one real portfolio. Convert one to a paid pilot.

ideas.title: Parametric Outage Cover for Satellite Internet Users
ideas.one_liner: A $60 probe network and parametric policy that pays cash when a satellite-dependent operation loses connectivity.
ideas.customer: Mines, farms, offshore and maritime fleets, remote clinics and construction firms whose operations run on a single LEO link.
ideas.problem: Insiders treat Starlink as a utility. Operator SLAs give small credits, while the customer's loss is stopped production, idle crews or a stalled remote-operations center. Insurers avoid the risk because they have no independent measurement.
ideas.solution: Ship a probe that actively tests the customer's link and cross-checks against a global mesh of other probes. That produces tamper-resistant uptime evidence. Sell a parametric policy that pays a fixed amount per hour beyond a threshold, underwritten by an MGA and reinsurers. Add failover advice and an independent uptime scorecard for SLA negotiation.
ideas.why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, and enterprise, maritime and rural operations now depend on it. A widely reported global outage in July 2025 (prior knowledge) showed correlated failure is real. Amazon and others are launching alternatives to fail over to.
ideas.revenue_model: Probe subscription $30-100 per month per site. Premium about 4-8% of annual connectivity spend once the policy launches. Data licensing to reinsurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Correlated single-vendor outages are actually easy to model, and the true blocker was measurement, not appetite. A cheap independent probe network converts an 'uninsurable' risk into a priced one.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the probe on a Raspberry Pi and deploy on 50 friendly terminals from RV, farm and maritime communities. Publish an uptime dashboard. Approach two MGAs about a pilot policy and sell probe subscriptions to three fleets.

ideas.title: Triage Software for Satellite-SOS Rescue Teams
ideas.one_liner: Intake, deduplication and dispatch software for county and volunteer search-and-rescue teams flooded by satellite SOS messages.
ideas.customer: County sheriff SAR coordinators, state SAR coordinators, national park services and mountain rescue organizations.
ideas.problem: As satellite texting reaches ordinary phones, more people go remote and press SOS. Rescuers receive short, delayed, asynchronous messages with weak location data and many false alarms. Coordination centers were built for 911 voice calls, and volunteer teams run on spreadsheets and group texts.
ideas.solution: A gateway that ingests SOS relays (email, API, text) from phone makers and satellite messaging providers, deduplicates, geolocates, and adds terrain and weather context. It runs structured 160-character question flows, recommends the resource type to dispatch, and keeps a log for after-action review and cost recovery.
ideas.why_now: Satellite messaging on unmodified phones went mainstream across 2025-26 (the briefing shows new carrier launches as late as Sept 28, 2026). AST and SpaceX D2C are scaling, and phone makers are adding satellite SOS. The receiving end has not been rebuilt.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-15k per year per county or team. State-level contracts of $50-200k. Optional paid membership or SAR-insurance partnership.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck moved from sending distress to receiving and triaging it. Whoever owns the receive-side workflow becomes the system of record, and public agencies pay for it out of existing rescue budgets.
ideas.first_30_days: Shadow three volunteer SAR teams and one state coordinator. Build a minimal intake and dedupe tool that runs alongside their current tools. Offer it free for one summer season in exchange for a paid annual contract.

ideas.title: Launch and Reentry Airspace Forecasts for Airlines
ideas.one_liner: A dispatcher-facing forecast of whether launch and debris closures will really happen, and what rerouting will cost.
ideas.customer: Airline operations control centers on Caribbean, Atlantic and Pacific routes, cargo airlines, business-jet operators and flight-planning software vendors.
ideas.problem: Launches hit 321 in 2025, and Starship debris in early 2025 disrupted flights around Florida and the Caribbean. Launch slips and scrubs make late notices unreliable. Dispatchers over-buffer fuel and time or get surprised, and there is no probabilistic view of hazard areas.
ideas.solution: An API and dashboard that fuses launch manifests, vehicle-specific slip and scrub statistics, trajectory and debris-response-area models, and reentry predictions. It outputs closure probability and expected reroute cost per flight. Deliver it into existing flight-planning tools as a plug-in.
ideas.why_now: Cadence is climbing (223 launches in 2023 to 321 in 2025), Starship is flying orbital profiles, and new vehicles such as New Glenn and Stoke's Nova are coming. Airspace impact scales with cadence.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-150k per year per airline. Per-flight API fees through flight-planning vendors. Cargo and charter tiers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The valuable prediction is not where the hazard area is but whether the launch will actually go, which is a schedule-slip model. That converts publicly available manifests into a decision-quality product.
ideas.first_30_days: Backtest a slip and scrub model on the last 12 months of Florida and Vandenberg launches. Show it to five dispatch managers at airlines flying Caribbean routes. Offer a free pilot on one route and a paid tier for the next quarter.

ideas.title: Thermosphere Density Nowcasts From Mega-Constellation Orbits
ideas.one_liner: A live atmospheric-drag API that uses the drag on thousands of satellites as a planetary sensor grid.
ideas.customer: Mid-size LEO operators, space situational awareness vendors (as an OEM component), launch providers, insurers, and reentry-risk teams.
ideas.problem: Drag uncertainty is the dominant error in LEO conjunction assessment and reentry prediction. With over 10,000 Starlinks in orbit and Solar Cycle 25 storms hitting low shells, operators face false-alarm maneuvers, wasted propellant and surprise reentries. Existing density models are coarse.
ideas.solution: Assimilate public element sets and published satellite ephemerides to infer density by altitude, latitude and time. Deliver a nowcast plus a 72-hour forecast as an API and as a plug-in for flight-dynamics tools. Sell reduced false-alarm rates and better reentry windows, with validation reports.
ideas.why_now: The mega-constellation means the sensors are already in orbit and free. The briefing reports about 10,413 Starlinks. Storm risk persists near the solar maximum. New operators are moving to lower shells and need better drag forecasts.
ideas.revenue_model: $50-250k per year per operator. OEM licensing to SSA vendors. Event-based storm reports for insurers and launch providers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: For space traffic, the sensor is not scarce, the model is. The largest calibration dataset ever assembled is flying overhead for free.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a backtest against public geomagnetic-storm episodes using open element sets, and publish accuracy versus a standard model. Offer free access to three mid-size operators and one SSA vendor in exchange for feedback and a paid pilot.

ideas.title: Verification Service for Satellite Imagery Authenticity
ideas.one_liner: Check whether a satellite image is real, and issue a chain-of-custody certificate for images used as evidence.
ideas.customer: Trade-finance banks and collateral managers, property and cargo insurers, sanctions and compliance teams, and newsroom verification desks.
ideas.problem: Generative AI can now fake satellite images, and fakes circulated during conflicts in 2025 (prior knowledge). Imagery is increasingly used as evidence for loans against stockpiles, insurance claims, sanctions cases and environmental claims. Fraud incentives rise with that value, and nobody certifies pixels.
ideas.solution: A verification API that checks a submitted image against multi-provider archives (free Sentinel and Landsat plus commercial partners) and physical consistency (sun angle, shadows, sensor geometry). Partners can sign images at ingestion with a provenance manifest. Deliver certified 'as-of' extracts for legal use.
ideas.why_now: Generative image quality crossed the threshold in 2025-26. Imagery archives are large and multi-source, and providers are looking for premium 'verified' tiers. The briefing notes decision products for regulated buyers remain open.
ideas.revenue_model: $20-200 per verification. Enterprise subscriptions of $30-150k per year. Revenue share with imagery providers on verified tiers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Detection models age quickly, but archive access does not. The moat is a cross-provider archive and provenance partnerships, not a classifier.
ideas.first_30_days: Assemble a test set of real and synthetic images. Build a reverse-lookup against Sentinel-2 and Landsat. Run free verifications for two commodity-finance firms and one newsroom, then convert one to a paid annual license.

ideas.title: Court-Ready Satellite Emission Evidence for Litigators
ideas.one_liner: Expert-witness-grade reports that use hourly geostationary pollution data to document emission events at large industrial sources.
ideas.customer: Environmental plaintiffs' firms, community groups with litigation funders, state attorney general offices, and insurers or investors assessing pollution liability.
ideas.problem: As federal enforcement priorities shifted in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), private litigation and state action fill the gap. Those actors need independent, admissible evidence, and most cannot interpret satellite data.
ideas.solution: Case-specific 'Emission Event Reports' for large point sources (power plants, refineries, LNG terminals, petrochemical complexes). They combine hourly NO2, SO2 and HCHO enhancements from geostationary sounders (NASA TEMPO in North America, Sentinel-4 in Europe), wind reanalysis and thermal flare data, with documented chain of custody and academic expert witnesses.
ideas.why_now: Hourly pollution monitoring from geostationary orbit is new: TEMPO has been operating since 2023-24 and Sentinel-4 launched in 2025. Regulatory retreat drives demand for private evidence.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-60k per case report. Retainer for firms with recurring dockets. Expert-testimony fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Litigation budgets grow when regulation shrinks. A method that survives a Daubert challenge is a defensible moat, because courts reward the first tested method.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with an atmospheric scientist willing to serve as expert. Build a report template on three well-known refinery or power-plant events. Present to five environmental plaintiffs' firms and one state AG office, and sign a first paid case.

ideas.title: Pre-Permitted Gateway Campuses for Satellite Constellations
ideas.one_liner: A real-estate developer for multi-tenant satellite gateway sites with power, fiber, interference studies and landing-right support.
ideas.customer: Constellation operators (broadband, direct-to-cell, EO downlink) that need dozens of gateways in many countries, and ground-station-as-a-service providers.
ideas.problem: Every constellation needs gateways that are radio-quiet, low in rain fade, and connected to fiber and power. Zoning, community opposition and national landing rights make site acquisition slow, and launching more satellites does not help if gateways are the bottleneck. AST is launch-constrained now, but ground capacity is next.
ideas.solution: Option, entitle and pre-permit 'gateway campuses' in strategic regions, then lease antenna pads on 10-15 year terms. Include interference and rain-fade studies, fiber and power, and local licensing help. Start in the Caribbean, Latin America and Africa, where landing rights and site scarcity bind hardest.
ideas.why_now: Launch capacity is exploding, so the bottleneck shifts to the ground. Spectrum is now owned by operators with big plans (SpaceX, AT&T, AST). Direct-to-cell needs many gateways to reach many carriers.
ideas.revenue_model: Pad leases $8-25k per month per antenna. Development fee on entitlement assignment. Long-term power and fiber pass-through margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Operators over-invest in satellites and under-invest in the boring ground sites that gate capacity. Zoning boards, not rockets, may be the binding constraint.
ideas.first_30_days: Use GIS to shortlist 30 parcels near fiber and power across five regions. Take low-cost options on five. Get LOIs from two gateway-hungry operators or teleport providers before spending on entitlements.

ideas.title: Dead-Zone Analytics to Price Satellite Add-Ons
ideas.one_liner: A tool that finds the small share of subscribers who will pay for satellite coverage, and prices it for them.
ideas.customer: Regional and mid-size mobile network operators and MVNOs launching satellite-to-phone services.
ideas.problem: Satellite-mobile partnerships are multiplying, but 'key questions remain unresolved' (Satellite Today, Sept 2026): carriers do not know how to price or differentiate them, and European operators disagree on their value. Giving the service away destroys value.
ideas.solution: Software that runs inside the operator's data environment and computes per-subscriber out-of-coverage dwell time and travel patterns. It segments buyers, runs price and offer experiments, and measures incremental ARPU and churn. It also tells network planners where satellite fills gaps more cheaply than a new site.
ideas.why_now: Deals with SpaceX, AST and others are now signed in bulk. Operators need to justify them commercially. SpaceX holds its own spectrum, which raises the stakes for carrier differentiation.
ideas.revenue_model: Revenue share of 5-10% of incremental add-on revenue, or a $/subscriber-year fee. Fixed-fee analytics packages for smaller operators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The value of satellite coverage is concentrated in perhaps 5-10% of subscribers who spend real time outside coverage (rural, hunters, truckers, boaters). Pricing to them beats a blanket giveaway.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one regional operator as a design partner. Run a free 60-day retrospective on anonymized coverage and dwell data, and show the segment size and revenue case. Convert to a pilot on real offers.

ideas.title: Licensing Workbench for Smallsat Operators
ideas.one_liner: A structured software system of record for satellite licensing across spectrum, debris, remote sensing and export control.
ideas.customer: Smallsat startups, university missions and new sovereign programs that currently pay law firms and consultants $50-300k per licensing cycle.
ideas.problem: Launches and deployments are at record levels (4,517 satellites in 2025), and licensing throughput is the hidden bottleneck. Operators juggle FCC, ITU, NOAA remote-sensing, debris-mitigation and export-control filings. Rules are changing (reported FCC rewrite, the 5-year deorbit rule, the proposed EU Space Act).
ideas.solution: A workbench with deterministic calculators (debris assessment, collision probability), templated filings, an ITU coordination tracker, deadline management and an insurer-ready data pack. Add a marketplace to hire specialist counsel. It is not a thin AI wrapper: the value is the structured filing data model and up-to-date rules.
ideas.why_now: The 2025-26 regulatory changes and a growing flood of new operators. The EU Space Act, FCC modernization and stricter debris rules all raise the compliance load.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-3k per month per mission. Per-filing fees. Referral fees from counsel and consultants.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Every launch boom makes regulatory throughput the binding constraint. The company that owns the data model of a filing becomes the system of record.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 15 smallsat licensing leads about their last filing. Build one calculator plus a deadline tracker for a specific filing, for example an FCC debris assessment. Sign five paying pilots at $500-1,000 per month.

ideas.title: Pooled Radiation Test Data for Commercial Chips
ideas.one_liner: A subscription database and beam-time broker so satellite builders stop each paying to test the same commercial chips.
ideas.customer: Constellation and smallsat builders using commercial parts, defense new-space suppliers, and chip vendors seeking space design wins.
ideas.problem: Proliferated constellations (Golden Dome's reported 600-satellite award, Starlink) run on commercial parts. Radiation-beam slots are scarce with multi-month queues, and results live in silos. Roughly the same popular parts get tested repeatedly.
ideas.solution: Pool member orders to buy block beam time at university and national facilities, and test the top parts by lot and date code. Publish a member-contributed database of results and anomalies, and broker custom tests. Members trade their data for access.
ideas.why_now: Defense demand for proliferated LEO and a wave of well-funded satellite makers are stressing limited test capacity. Commercial-parts-first design is now standard.
ideas.revenue_model: $10-50k per year per member. 10-15% fee on brokered custom tests. Sponsored testing from chip vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a commercial-parts space industry, test data is the scarce asset, not the parts. The group that pools it becomes the standards-setter.
ideas.first_30_days: Contact two beam facilities about block-time pricing. Pre-sell five founding memberships to satellite builders at $10k each. Publish a free first report on one popular microcontroller or memory part to establish credibility.

ideas.title: Calibration Target Network for Earth-Observation Startups
ideas.one_liner: Networked ground calibration targets that issue overpass-synchronized calibration certificates for EO satellites.
ideas.customer: EO and SAR constellation operators, analytics firms selling certified measurements (insurance, methane, deforestation), and government agencies.
ideas.problem: Every new imaging satellite needs geometric and radiometric calibration, mostly done ad hoc. As EO output becomes regulated evidence, buyers ask who certified the sensor, and no third party provides traceable, on-demand ground truth.
ideas.solution: Deploy SAR corner reflectors, spectral tarps and instrumented sites (GPS, weather, irradiance) at a handful of stable locations. Automatically log each satellite overpass and issue a calibration certificate. Offer custom validation sites and controlled-release campaigns for customers.
ideas.why_now: The EO sector is mature and government-anchored (Planet's large contracts and Pelican production doubling per the briefing). Regulated uses raise demand for traceability. Many new SAR and hyperspectral entrants launch each year.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-150k per year per constellation. Project fees for custom validation sites. Certificates sold to analytics customers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: As EO becomes evidence, the bottleneck is ground presence synchronized with overpasses, not more data.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two well-known desert sites and place a first set of low-cost reflectors and tarps. Offer free certificates to three SAR and optical startups in return for testimonials, and ask for paid annual plans after the first quarter.

ideas.title: Sovereign Data Vaults in Orbit
ideas.one_liner: Encrypted national-records backups stored in orbit, out of reach of seizure, cyber-wipe or flood.
ideas.customer: Governments of small, exposed or at-risk states (Baltics, Pacific island nations, Ukraine, Taiwan-type buyers), central banks and national archives.
ideas.problem: Countries already run 'data embassies' in friendly data centers, but those still sit on someone's soil. A wipe, seizure, war or sea-level loss can strand civil registries, land titles and treasury records.
ideas.solution: Start with a hosted-payload vault on a partner satellite: an append-only, radiation-tolerant encrypted store holding registries and legal records, with keys held by the customer under multi-party control and a dead-man retrieval process. Grow into dedicated vault satellites.
ideas.why_now: Rideshare pricing makes small payloads cheap. 2025 demonstrations of storage and compute in orbit (Lonestar's data payloads, Starcloud's reported H100 launch) showed the concept works. Geopolitical risk to state data has risen.
ideas.revenue_model: Feasibility studies $50-150k. Multi-year vault contracts of $1-5M per year. Per-TB-year storage fees after launch.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Governments already pay for offshore backups. The extraterritorial jurisdiction of orbit can be sold as a legal and physical guarantee, not as a gadget.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach digital-government offices in Estonia, Tuvalu, Ukraine and Taiwan-type buyers with a paid feasibility study. Line up a hosted-payload slot with an existing operator. Design the key-custody model with a legal adviser on treaty and jurisdiction questions.

ideas.title: GPS Spoofing Alarm Using LEO Signals
ideas.one_liner: A passive receiver that listens to Starlink, OneWeb and Iridium-style signals and flags when GPS disagrees.
ideas.customer: Shipping companies and port authorities in jammed regions (Baltic, Persian Gulf, Red Sea), aviation operators, telecom timing operators, drone fleets, and hull and P&I insurers.
ideas.problem: GNSS jamming and spoofing have spread across shipping and aviation (prior knowledge, 2024-25). Most detection depends on GNSS itself or expensive inertial systems. Operators and insurers want independent evidence of position integrity.
ideas.solution: A small software-defined receiver that measures Doppler and timing from LEO communication signals of opportunity and, using public orbit data, checks position and time consistency. First product is an integrity alarm, not a navigator. Later add tens-of-meters holdover navigation.
ideas.why_now: There are about 10,000 Starlinks plus other constellations, so signals of opportunity are abundant. Academic demonstrations of positioning from them have matured. Jamming has moved from a defense concern to a commercial one.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k per unit plus $100 per month cloud analytics. Insurer-funded fleet programs. Government pilots.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: You do not need to navigate better than GPS to be valuable, only to disagree with it reliably. Integrity is a cheaper, faster product than replacement navigation.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a lab proof of concept using a Ku-band LNB and an SDR. Recruit two Baltic or Gulf ship managers or port operators for field trials. Approach one marine insurer about premium credits for verified integrity.

ideas.title: Global Rain Radar From Starlink Dishes
ideas.one_liner: Turn opted-in Starlink terminals into the densest rain-gauge network ever built and sell ground-truth rainfall to insurers.
ideas.customer: Parametric crop and flood insurers and MGAs, reinsurers, agricultural cooperatives, utilities and municipal flood teams.
ideas.problem: Rain gauges are sparse and radar coverage is poor in rural and developing regions. Parametric insurance suffers from basis risk, and disputes arise when the index does not match what happened at the field.
ideas.solution: An open-source agent reads a terminal's local signal telemetry, correlates rain-induced attenuation with rain rate, and produces minute-level hyperlocal rainfall. Owners opt in and receive a monthly credit. Sell the result as an API and as audited trigger data for parametric products.
ideas.why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, including many rural users. The idea of using satellite-link attenuation as a rain sensor is established in research. Parametric insurance is growing, and public radar and gauge budgets are under pressure.
ideas.revenue_model: API subscriptions $20-200k per year per insurer or cooperative. Per-trigger data fees. Owner credits of $2-5 per month as the cost of goods.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rain fade is a nuisance to network engineers but a measurement to meteorologists. The sensors are already installed and paid for by their owners.
ideas.first_30_days: Adapt open-source telemetry tools and recruit 300 terminal owners with a small credit. Co-locate with 30 tipping-bucket gauges and publish a validation note. Pitch two parametric MGAs and one agricultural cooperative, and plan a fallback if SpaceX restricts local access.

ideas.title: Subsurface Desert Mapping From Free Radar Satellites
ideas.one_liner: Use open L-band radar data to map buried channels and structures beneath arid ground for mineral and water explorers.
ideas.customer: Junior critical-mineral explorers, uranium and lithium prospectors, groundwater drillers, national geological surveys and arid-region water utilities.
ideas.problem: Exploration in deserts costs a fortune per drill hole, targeting is often guesswork, and airborne geophysics is expensive. Explorers need cheaper first-pass targeting.
ideas.solution: Combine weekly-repeat NISAR L-band radar (open data), Sentinel-1 and, outside North America and Europe, ESA Biomass P-band to map buried paleo-channels, faults and shallow structure in hyper-arid terrain. Deliver target packages per license block, plus a success-fee option.
ideas.why_now: NISAR launched in July 2025 with an open-data policy, and ESA's Biomass P-band radar launched in April 2025. Demand for critical minerals is at a peak. Radar penetration only works in very dry ground, so scope is narrow but valuable.
ideas.revenue_model: $20-60k per license block. Success fee or royalty on discoveries. Annual subscriptions for geological surveys.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Seeing beneath sand from orbit sounds like science fiction, and it is now possible with free data. The business is expertise and interpretation, not satellites.
