It cuts nickel strips, pulls cells, tests each one (IR and impedance), grades A/B/C, and repackages A-grade cells for stationary storage or tools. C-grade goes to recyclers. It starts as a manual-plus-robotic service in one city.
ideas.why_now: 2025-26 robot foundation models made unstructured manipulation tasks feasible, and e-bike fire scrutiny gives fleets a reason to pay.
ideas.revenue_model: Fee per pack processed, plus margin on graded cells, plus recycler payments for C-grade.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Recyclers built for EV packs face feed that is 15 years late. E-bike packs are small enough that a robot cell amortizes quickly, and their cells are far from dead.
ideas.first_30_days: Contract with 2 fleet operators or a swap network in NYC or LA. Rent a bench with a fire-safe enclosure and cell testers. Process 500 packs manually to build the dataset and unit economics before adding the robot.

ideas.title: Protein Cartridges for Heavy Rare-Earth Polishing
ideas.one_liner: Skid-mounted cartridges of engineered lanmodulin-type proteins that separate heavy rare earths (Dy, Tb) from magnet-recycling leachate without long solvent-extraction chains.
ideas.customer: Magnet recyclers and small separators whose processes end in mixed rare-earth concentrates, plus DoD- and DOE-backed pilot programs.
ideas.problem: Recovery projects often end with mixed concentrates that still need separation, which conventionally takes hundreds of solvent-extraction stages that China dominates. Heavy rare earths are the acute chokepoint after China's 2025 export controls.
ideas.solution: Protein-based sorbents (naturally lanthanide-binding proteins, studied at Penn State and Lawrence Livermore) engineered for heavy-RE selectivity. They are packed in modular columns as a polishing step at ambient conditions. The business model is cartridge consumables plus skid rental.
ideas.why_now: Heavy rare earths are now a stated national-security bottleneck, DOE announced $134M for demonstrations in June 2026, and AI protein design has made engineering selectivity a computation problem instead of a decade-long screen.
ideas.revenue_model: Consumable cartridge sales plus skid lease. Early revenue from SBIR grants and paid pilots.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth chemistry fights in a sea of near-identical ions, while proteins evolved to tell lanthanides apart. The hard part is now designing the scaffold, not discovering the effect.
ideas.first_30_days: License or partner with a university lab. Run bench tests on real recycler leachate. Apply to DOE and DoD SBIR programs. Sign 2 recyclers to paid pilots.

ideas.title: EU Liable-Party-of-Record for AI Products
ideas.one_liner: The registered agent of the AI era: an insured EU entity that stands as authorised representative under the new Product Liability Directive and keeps clients' evidence court-ready.
ideas.customer: Non-EU makers (10-200 staff) of AI-enabled consumer hardware and apps, such as robot vacuums, wearables, AI toys, smart-home and e-mobility firmware, selling into the EU via Amazon, Shopify or retailers.
ideas.problem: From 9 Dec 2026 software and AI count as 'products' under Directive 2024/2853. Courts can order disclosure of evidence, a defendant who stonewalls faces a presumption of defect, and liability cascades to importers, authorised representatives and fulfilment providers when no EU manufacturer exists. Small non-EU firms have no solvent EU counterparty, no organised technical file, and no cover. Marketplaces and logistics partners will start demanding all three.
ideas.solution: A fixed-fee service with four parts. (1) An EU entity acting as authorised representative and liable operator of record. (2) A 'disclosure-ready dossier': model and version registry, safety case, incident and OTA-update logs, and retention rules, collected through simple exports so a court order can be met in days. (3) EU-language complaint and defect intake plus recall coordination. (4) A bundled PLD policy through a fronting carrier or MGA, priced lower because the dossier removes unknowns.
ideas.why_now: The transposition deadline is 9 Dec 2026, about ten weeks away, and products placed on the market after it fall under the new regime. Only a minority of member states have finished transposing, so uncertainty peaks now. The December 2024 GPSR rule created a wave of paid 'EU responsible person' services, which shows small sellers buy this kind of compliance. Carriers filing broad AI exclusions (AIG, Berkley, Great American, ISO CG 40 47/48) push AI firms toward affirmative cover.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5k-6k per month per client by risk tier, a $5-15k onboarding fee for the dossier, 10-15% commission on the bundled policy, and incident-response retainers. 40 clients at about $3k per month is roughly $1.4M ARR.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The PLD creates an evidence-access war (disclosure orders plus presumptions of defect), and small firms lose it by default because they cannot produce coherent records. What clients buy is not legal advice but a solvent, present EU party who can hand a court a clean file. Demand will arrive through the distribution chain first, because retailers and marketplaces will impose it by contract before any regulator enforces it.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with an EU product-liability law firm (NL, IE or DE) for the entity and an opinion letter. Publish a 10-page 'PLD readiness for AI hardware' guide. Pitch it to GPSR-rep leads, hardware accelerator alumni and Amazon/Shopify hardware sellers. Sign 5 founding clients at $1k per month. Get one European MGA or Lloyd's coverholder to quote the bundled policy.

ideas.title: Contingency Subrogation Forensics for Robot Accidents
ideas.one_liner: CCC-for-robots: a forensic recovery shop that turns warehouse-robot, AV and drone logs into fault-apportioned recovery demands for the insurers who already paid the claim.
ideas.customer: Subrogation units and TPAs at mid-size commercial P&C carriers, warehouse-focused MGAs, and brokers serving 3PLs and logistics parks.
ideas.problem: Robots damage racking, inventory, vehicles and people, and the insurer pays first, often under a policy never rated for robots. Recovery depends on whether the hardware, the model, the integrator's configuration, the operator's procedure or maintenance failed. The evidence sits in vendor-controlled logs and cloud consoles that get purged, and vendor contracts cap liability and force arbitration. Adjusters do not know what to ask for or how fast.
ideas.solution: A standard 72-hour evidence-preservation and vendor data-request package. Log parsers for the export formats of 3-5 common AMR, AGV, forklift and robotaxi platforms. A reconstruction timeline. A fault-apportionment matrix (OEM, integrator, operator, maintainer, site) with contract-cap analysis, plus a demand package addressed to the vendor's insurer.
ideas.why_now: Warehouse robot fleets, many of them imported, are scaling faster than underwriters' understanding, and trade press says insurers are unprepared. Robotaxi fleets are expanding across US cities in 2026. Carriers adding AI exclusions to GL, E&O and EPLI make 'which policy pays' a live dispute, which raises the value of recovering the loss from someone else. Claims from 2024-25 deployments are now maturing into subrogation files.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-8k flat fee per file plus 15-25% contingency on recoveries above a threshold. Later, annual retainers with carriers and a licensed evidence-request tool for adjusters.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The first real price of AI and robot liability will be set in recovery negotiations, not in underwriting. Whoever standardises how blame is split between OEM, integrator and operator, and holds the resulting loss-cost data, becomes the rating bureau, as CCC and Verisk did in auto. The bottleneck is evidence access and speed, not legal theory.
ideas.first_30_days: Email 30 subrogation managers and TPAs offering a free reconstruction and recovery memo on one closed robot or AV claim within 10 days. Bring on an ex-robotics field-service engineer and subrogation counsel on a retainer. Write the preservation-letter pack. Aim for 2 paid files by day 60.

ideas.title: Legal Defense Plan for Human-in-the-Loop Workers
ideas.one_liner: A USCCA-style membership that protects the nurse, safety driver or loan officer who gets blamed when AI recommends and a human signs, plus an 'override receipt' log the member personally owns.
ideas.customer: Unions, state nurses' associations and professional societies (radiologic technologists, CRNAs, claims adjusters, AV teleoperators and safety drivers) as distribution partners. Members pay through a dues add-on, or employers buy it as a retention benefit.
ideas.problem: Regulations and enterprise policies demand 'meaningful human oversight', which in practice makes the human the liability sponge, the 'moral crumple zone'. Uber's Tempe safety driver was criminally charged, and nurse RaDonda Vaught was convicted after overriding an automated dispensing cabinet. Employer indemnities and malpractice policies rarely cover AI-specific disputes, licensing-board action, or retaliation for raising concerns.
ideas.solution: (1) A prepaid legal defense retainer covering civil, licensing-board and criminal matters, with panel counsel experienced in tech-mediated harm. (2) 'Override receipts': a light app or extension where the member logs each override, disagreement or safety concern, with hashed timestamps in a member-owned escrow. (3) Plain-English 'working with this AI tool' duty briefings per workplace system. (4) Aggregated, anonymised incident data that gives unions leverage in bargaining over staffing and AI use.
ideas.why_now: AI decision support is now standard in hospitals (sepsis alerts, ambient scribes) and in robotaxi remote operations. Human-oversight duties are being written into the EU AI Act and state laws. Insurers' AI exclusions signal to employers that AI losses may be uninsured, so risk will be pushed down to individual workers. Unions are actively bargaining over AI in 2025-26.
ideas.revenue_model: $9-19 per member per month through associations, with margin after panel counsel and a reinsurer or legal-plan administrator. Employer-paid group plans and individual upsells.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The person who actually absorbs AI risk is neither the deployer nor the vendor but the individual signer, and no product exists for them. Unions already have distribution and every reason to buy. The override-receipt record may be worth more than the defense cover, because it is the human-oversight evidence courts will look for, and it hands the union data on unsafe deployments.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one narrow group, such as AV teleoperators and safety drivers or nurses in one state. Get an MOU with one union local or association. Retain a defense-firm panel at group rates. Ship the override log as a Chrome extension or SMS bot. Pre-sell 300 members at $12 per month, and check state prepaid-legal-plan rules first.

ideas.title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
ideas.one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
ideas.customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
ideas.problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
ideas.solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
ideas.why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
ideas.revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.

ideas.title: Independent-Pricing Ledger for Algorithmic Antitrust Risk
ideas.one_liner: A neutral logbook beside revenue-management software that proves humans set rents and room rates independently, and doubles as the underwriting file for algorithmic-collusion defense cover.
ideas.customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (2k-25k units), hotel groups and self-storage and student-housing operators using shared-pricing algorithms, plus their antitrust counsel and D&O or defense-cost carriers.
ideas.problem: The DOJ's RealPage settlement (Nov 2025) bars use of competitors' nonpublic data and alignment of prices. California and New York banned algorithmic rent-setting in Oct 2025. Class actions continue against landlords, not just vendors. Liability turns on whether users set prices independently or rubber-stamped a pooled tool, and on data provenance. Operators cannot produce that evidence, and carriers will not underwrite defense costs without it.
ideas.solution: A light ledger fed by exports or APIs from Yardi, RealPage, Entrata, Duetto and similar tools. It records recommended versus adopted price, override reason codes and data-provenance flags. It produces a quarterly 'independence attestation' reviewed by an outside economist, includes a simulator showing the revenue cost of overriding (often small), and packages an underwriting-grade file for defense-cost cover. Design it under counsel's privilege from day one.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement plus new state and city laws hit in late 2025 and 2026, and the settlements set monitoring expectations. Mid-market operators are the next wave of defendants and cannot afford bespoke audits. Insurers are simultaneously narrowing AI and antitrust cover.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.50-4 per unit per year (about $6-20k for a 5k-unit operator), $10-25k per year for economist attestation, and 10-15% of the defense-cost premium placed.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The legal variable is not the algorithm's accuracy but its acceptance rate and data provenance, and both are just logs. Evidence must exist before the subpoena arrives. The ledger also becomes the first actuarial dataset for algorithmic-antitrust risk, which no carrier has.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with an ex-DOJ or FTC economist and an antitrust boutique. Build CSV-only ingestion for two property-management systems. Approach 10 mid-size operators through a National Apartment Association state affiliate and their counsel. Sell a $7.5k 'independence audit' of the last 12 months of pricing decisions as the entry product, delivered services-first.

ideas.title: Robot Finger That Makes Legacy Instruments Agent-Operable
ideas.one_liner: A camera-plus-servo retrofit box that presses buttons, turns knobs and reads displays on validated lab and test equipment from the outside, giving decade-old instruments an API without touching their software.
ideas.customer: QC and analytical labs in pharma and CDMOs, food and environmental testing labs, university core facilities, and small biotechs running out-of-support equipment such as plate readers, autoclaves, centrifuges, HPLC pumps, stability chambers and test benches.
ideas.problem: Lab automation assumes new, API-enabled instruments, but the installed base is 10-20-year-old boxes with front panels only. In GxP and ISO 17025 labs, changing instrument firmware or software can trigger revalidation, which blocks IT-style integration. Scientists and agents still want unattended overnight runs, scheduling and structured logs.
ideas.solution: A clamp-on or adhesive module with 2-6 servos for buttons, knobs and a touchscreen stylus, a wide-angle camera, and a vision-language model that reads 7-segment displays, LCDs and status LEDs. A confirm-after-every-action loop and hard interlocks make it safe. It exposes an MCP and REST endpoint ('start program 4', 'read temperature', 'log state') and keeps video plus state log as the audit trail. It sits outside the validated boundary as 'operator-equivalent', so only the actuator needs qualification.
ideas.why_now: Vision-language models now read messy panels cheaply and reliably, and servo and edge-compute costs are trivial. Autonomous-lab offerings such as Ginkgo Cloud Lab prove scientists want agent-run experiments, but they require shipping samples to a vendor's lab. Most labs still own and must keep using their own equipment.
ideas.revenue_model: $400-900 hardware per instrument, $40-100 per month per device for scheduling, audit trail and the agent endpoint, and $2-5k per site for IQ/OQ qualification templates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Revalidation cost, not technology, blocks lab automation. An actuator that does exactly what a technician's finger does sidesteps change control, so selling 'validation-friendly' beats selling 'smart'. The video-verified state log is also a better audit trail than most instruments produce natively.
ideas.first_30_days: Build 3 prototypes from off-the-shelf servos, cameras and a Raspberry Pi-class board. Interview 20 QC lab managers and core-facility directors. Offer free two-week pilots on one autoclave or plate reader that runs a nightly routine, then convert to a $3k paid pilot including an IQ/OQ document.

ideas.title: Permit-as-Firmware Groundwater Pump Governor
ideas.one_liner: A smart pump controller that hard-enforces a farmer's groundwater allocation and lets an agent trade unused acre-feet with neighbors before the pump ever exceeds its limit.
ideas.customer: Irrigated growers (almonds, pistachios, alfalfa, wine grapes) in California's regulated groundwater basins, especially San Joaquin Valley subbasins with adopted allocations and overpumping penalties. Groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) are the channel and co-payer.
ideas.problem: Allocations are enforced after the fact from meter reads. Kings County's agency, for example, set a $500-per-acre-foot charge for pumping above base allocation, with penalties slated after the 2026 water year. Probationary subbasins (Tule, Tulare Lake) add $300-per-well registration and a $20-per-acre-foot state fee. Farmers overshoot by accident, water trades run through brokers and phone calls, and GSAs cannot verify compliance without costly audits.
ideas.solution: A retrofit device on the well's starter or VFD, tied to a certified flow-meter reader, keeping a live allocation ledger. It soft-throttles as the budget nears zero, and can hard-stop with a paid override that 'borrows' at the penalty price. The grower's dashboard or agent can pre-bid to buy or sell units on a subbasin exchange. The GSA receives a read-only, tamper-evident compliance feed and can give fee discounts for participating wells.
ideas.why_now: Allocation-based enforcement begins in earnest with the 2027 water year, and the state has already put two San Joaquin Valley subbasins on probation. Water prices and fallowing pressure make trading valuable. Cellular and LoRa IoT and smart motor starters are now cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5-3k per well install, $50-150 per month per well, a 1-2% fee on water trades, and GSA grants or fee credits that subsidise compliance metering.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The law is already a constraint. The product turns a legal budget into a physical budget, like a hard credit limit on a card. Growers want the stop because it converts unpredictable $500-per-acre-foot penalties into a controllable budget, and GSAs want it because self-reporting becomes verified data. Sell it as insurance against fines, not as smart irrigation.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one subbasin with adopted allocations and penalties. Recruit 3 pump-service companies as install partners, since they own the relationship with the well. Pilot free on 5 wells in exchange for testimonials and data. Ask the GSA general manager for a compliance-metering pilot grant.

ideas.title: Programmable Lockbox for GPU and Robot Collateral
ideas.one_liner: Tri-party custody software and hardware that lets lenders verify, and if needed take over, financed GPU clusters and robot fleets sitting in someone else's building.
ideas.customer: Specialty and private-credit lenders and equipment lessors financing GPU clouds and robots-as-a-service. Borrowers such as neoclouds and robot operators pay to lower their borrowing spread, and colo operators act as a channel.
ideas.problem: More than $20B of loans are now secured by GPUs, and H100-class rental rates fell from about $7-10 per hour in early 2024 to $2-4 by late 2025, so lenders must know whether machines exist, are powered and utilised, and are not double-pledged. Monitoring today is a spreadsheet plus quarterly audits. The bigger trapdoors are the colo landlord's lien for unpaid power or rent and who physically or remotely controls the hardware on default.
ideas.solution: (1) A continuous collateral-health feed: hardware serials and attestation (TPM or GPU attestation where available), BMC and out-of-band data, power-meter readings, latency-based geolocation, and periodic photo audits by colo remote hands. (2) Escrowed step-in credentials for BMC and fleet consoles, plus a tri-party lockbox agreement with the colo covering access and lien waivers, with API-triggered 'freeze' and 'transfer to lender' modes. (3) Standard borrowing-base reports.
ideas.why_now: GPU-collateralised private credit scaled from almost nothing to over $20B in about two years, with loans maturing 2026-2028 among a small, correlated lender group. Banks avoid the fast-depreciating collateral, leaving private credit to fill the gap. Utilisation and location risk is now board-level for lenders. Robot-as-a-service leasing needs the same control layer.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40 per GPU or robot per month paid by the borrower, or 10-25 bps on outstanding facility size, plus a $25k onboarding fee per facility and colo referral fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Lender losses come from control failures such as liens, access and double-pledging, not from chips vanishing. Contracts plus access-control APIs solve most of it. The borrower is the real buyer, because a 50-100 bps lower spread beats the fee, so sell it to the neocloud CFO as a rate reduction.
ideas.first_30_days: Speak with 15 specialty lenders and equipment-finance boutiques and 10 GPU-cloud CFOs. Sell a manual 'collateral control audit' at $15-30k for two facilities. Draft the tri-party lockbox template with a finance lawyer, then productise the attestation feed.

ideas.title: Universal Robot Cone: Vendor-Neutral Keep-Out Zones
ideas.one_liner: One tap, or one cheap beacon dropped on the floor, creates a temporary no-go zone that every robot brand in the building obeys, with a log to prove it.
ideas.customer: 3PL and warehouse operators and hospital operations teams running multi-vendor AMRs, AGVs and autonomous scrubbers or forklifts, especially their safety managers and insurers.
ideas.problem: Mixed fleets each have their own fleet manager and zone tool. A worker who finds a spill, opens a lift or spots a person in an aisle cannot instantly stop every robot across vendors. E-stops are vendor-specific and incident evidence is fragmented. Existing standards cover fleet control (VDA 5050) or monitoring (MassRobotics), but neither provides a neutral, human-triggered safety boundary.
ideas.solution: Phase 1 is software: a tablet or wearable app that pushes a temporary keep-out polygon, with expiry and audit, to each vendor's fleet-manager API at once. Phase 2 is a $60-100 BLE/UWB and visual-marker beacon 'cone' that creates dynamic zones, with an open spec pitched to standards bodies. A neutral log records who created and cleared each zone and which robots entered it.
ideas.why_now: Multi-vendor fleets, many imported, are now normal in large warehouses and insurers say they are unprepared. VDA 5050 and MassRobotics adapters make cross-vendor integration feasible. ISO 3691-4 audits and rising incident claims give safety managers budget.
ideas.revenue_model: $300-800 per site per month for the software, about $75 per beacon, integration or certification fees from robot OEMs who want 'cone-compatible' status, and possible insurer premium discounts shared with customers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The safety stop line is the one thing every vendor must honor and the one thing no vendor wants to own across competitors. Whoever owns the neutral stop line owns the cross-vendor safety log, which becomes the reference record in any liability dispute.
ideas.first_30_days: Visit 10 warehouses running two or more robot vendors. Build adapters for two or three fleet APIs with open documentation. Run a paid pilot with one 3PL at $500 per month, used in a safety drill. Ask the site's broker for an endorsement letter.

ideas.title: Chaos Testing for Buildings as Code-Required Commissioning
ideas.one_liner: An agent that safely actuates a building's HVAC at night, forcing dampers, valves and pumps through scripted step tests, to produce the functional-test evidence that codes require and passive analytics cannot.
ideas.customer: Commissioning firms and energy-service companies, and owners of 100k-2M sq ft commercial buildings facing performance standards (NYC Local Law 97, Washington and Denver building performance standards) and California Title 24 acceptance testing.
ideas.problem: Passive fault-detection analytics cannot tell 'stuck damper' from 'no demand'. Functional performance tests are still done by hand on clipboards at handover and rarely repeated, so buildings drift into waste. Emissions penalties and code-required acceptance tests raise the stakes, yet commissioning agents are labor-constrained.
ideas.solution: Connect through a BACnet or BAS gateway with read/write access. An LLM converts Sequences of Operation (ASHRAE Guideline 36 or project spec PDFs) into bounded test scripts with safety envelopes and automatic rollback. Overnight runs produce pass/fail results with evidence, a deficiency list with estimated savings, and signed test reports for compliance. Re-run quarterly, with operator approval built in.
ideas.why_now: BAS gateways and cloud connections are mainstream. LLMs can now parse sequences and generate test logic. Building performance standards, including LL97, are producing real penalties, and utilities pay for measured savings. Commissioning firms cannot hire enough engineers.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-15k per building test campaign, $1-3k per month for ongoing quarterly testing, white-label resale through commissioning firms at about 30% margin, and shared-savings deals with ESCOs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Active probing creates ground-truth labels that passive analytics lack, and the law already requires many of the tests, so automating them cuts a mandatory cost rather than selling a discretionary energy project. Chaos engineering is routine in software but almost unknown in buildings because nobody trusts write access, so the real product is the safety envelope, rollback and operator sign-off, more than the AI.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with two commissioning-authority firms. Agree on five common tests (economizer, VAV minimum flow, chiller staging, sensor cross-checks, pump changeover). Run them on 3 buildings with BACnet access at a fixed fee priced at 40-60% of a manual test, and document the energy findings.

ideas.title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
ideas.one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
ideas.customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
ideas.problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
ideas.solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
ideas.why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Pitch three mid-size dating, gig or cannabis-tech platforms and one cyber MGA. Offer a free 90-day pilot against one vendor under NDA. Publish an anonymised benchmark from the pilot to generate inbound.

ideas.title: Reliance Ratings for SOC 2 Reports and Auditors
ideas.one_liner: A buyer-paid forensic desk that tells vendor-risk teams how far to trust a given SOC 2 or ISO report, and the audit firm that signed it.
ideas.customer: Third-party-risk and security teams at banks, health systems, insurers and mid-market SaaS companies that ingest hundreds of vendor reports a year. Cyber insurers and PE/VC diligence teams are the second wave.
ideas.problem: In March 2026 a whistleblower alleged that Delve, a YC-backed startup valued at about $300M, issued 494 near-identical SOC 2 reports with conclusions pre-filled and signed by two rubber-stamp firms. YC removed it in April, and Delve disputes the claims. Buyers now suspect every clean PDF. Manual checks of AICPA peer-review and NASBA licence records take about 30 minutes per report, so most teams skip them.
ideas.solution: The buyer uploads the vendor's report. We compare it with a growing corpus using fuzzy fingerprints of system descriptions, test procedures and exception language. We check CPA licence, AICPA peer-review status, firm ownership, address and staffing footprint, sample sizes, period length, carve-outs and subservice-organisation scope. Output is a reliance score, a one-page red-flag memo, and a continuously updated rating of audit firms based on exception rates, boilerplate share and peer-review opinions.
ideas.why_now: The Delve fallout in spring 2026 made every security team ask 'who signed this?'. Compliance-automation platforms now tie vendors to audit-firm networks at scale (Vanta reports about 16,000 customers). LLMs make reading and comparing thousands of 80-page reports cheap for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: $200-400 per report on demand, $20-60k per year TPRM subscriptions, API licences to vendor-risk platforms, and insurer portfolio scans.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat the audit as a commodity input that automation has solved. Audit quality varies enormously and invisibly, and the vendor pays its own auditor. That is the same conflict that made bond-rating agencies necessary. The moat is the corpus of reports, which only buyers collectively hold.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the fingerprint tool on 200 public reports from trust centres. Publish an 'Auditor Firm Quality Index v0' from public peer-review data. Offer security leads free re-verification of their vendor stack in exchange for contributing reports to the corpus, starting with those exposed to Delve's customer list.

ideas.title: AI-Washing Forensics for Investors and Buyers
ideas.one_liner: A five-day outside-in diligence product that tests whether an AI startup's product is real autonomy, its revenue is real, and its users are human.
ideas.customer: Seed-to-growth investors (micro-VCs, corporate VCs, growth funds), corporate M&A teams, venture lenders, and enterprise procurement teams buying AI vendors.
ideas.problem: Builder.ai's 2025 insolvency (marketed AI, with heavy human labour behind it), the 2025 DOJ case against the founder of Nate, and a wave of 'ARR' made of pilots, credits and bot traffic show that diligence rests on demos, reference calls and a quality-of-earnings that never tests the technology claim.
ideas.solution: A black-box harness and data-room protocol. It covers interaction testing at scale (latency and variance signatures that reveal human-in-the-loop or third-party model calls), unit-economics reconstruction (tokens versus price versus gross margin), revenue reality (read-only Stripe and bank data plus contract sampling to separate pilot, committed, credit-funded and refunded revenue), audience authenticity (bot and agent share of users from server logs), and independent reference call-backs. Output is a 'Reality Report' with confidence intervals.
ideas.why_now: Builder.ai (2025) and Delve (2026) reset investor trust. AI-startup ARR claims are exploding, and more than half of web traffic is now automated, which inflates 'users'. Investors are compressing diligence to days, and AI products are uniquely testable from outside because you can hit the endpoint.
ideas.revenue_model: $15-40k per full report paid by the investor (often reimbursed at close), a $5k lite scan, and annual portfolio-monitoring retainers for funds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume diligence must rely on the founder's data. AI products can be tested from the outside, so the scarce thing is independence and speed, and the buyer of speed is an investor with a 48-hour exclusivity window.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer five free 'reality scans' to angel syndicates and micro-VC partners on live deals in exchange for named case studies. Build the harness with two ML engineers and one forensic accountant. Set pricing after three wins.

ideas.title: Notary-Witnessed Hiring Against Deepfake Candidates
ideas.one_liner: On-demand licensed notaries sit beside a remote candidate for the final interview or day-one onboarding and sign an attestation.
ideas.customer: Security and talent leads at remote-first software, fintech and defence-contractor employers, plus technical recruiting agencies, staffing firms and employer-of-record providers.
ideas.problem: An August 2026 eleven-nation advisory warned that North Korean IT-worker operations use real-time deepfakes to beat hiring checks, with 6,500+ similar cases reported globally. Employers face sanctions exposure. Liveness and document checks are being defeated, and the only alternatives are flying candidates in or trusting software.
ideas.solution: A marketplace and quality layer over existing mobile notaries and I-9 authorised representatives. A candidate books a witnessed final round in their own city. The witness checks ID, sweeps the room and desk for second screens and earpieces, positions a second camera, and signs a sealed attestation. An optional witnessed live-coding session runs on a locked, company-supplied laptop. A second 10-minute witnessed check at day 30 confirms identity continuity. Coverage starts in 200 US metros and expands to the UK and EU.
ideas.why_now: Real-time deepfake interviews are now mainstream and the 11-nation advisory (Aug 2026) is prompting boards to act. The DHS remote I-9 alternative procedure already blesses human 'authorised representatives'. Mobile signing agents lost volume when mortgage origination slumped, so witness supply is cheap.
ideas.revenue_model: $150-350 per witnessed session (about 60% to the witness), $2-10k per month enterprise subscriptions, and a per-hire fee for staffing agencies.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Insiders think software has to beat deepfakes. For high-stakes moments, the cheapest defence is physics. A $200 human in the room costs less than one failed hire, and the scarce input is legally recognised people who already verify identity for a living. There are millions of commissioned US notaries.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 40 notaries and loan-signing agents in five metros through signing-agent communities. Write a witness protocol and kit checklist, with legal review of what a notary may attest outside a notarial act. Pilot with three staffing firms or security-conscious startups.

ideas.title: Bonded Claims: Bug Bounties for Product Labels
ideas.one_liner: Brands post a forfeitable bond behind a testable label claim, and anyone can buy the product, get it lab-tested and collect the bond if the claim is false.
ideas.customer: Mid-size DTC supplement, protein, baby-food and pet-food brands whose 'third-party tested' or 'heavy-metal free' claims are doubted, plus retail and marketplace buyers who want evidence and insurers.
ideas.problem: Label claims cannot be checked on the shelf. Certifications are one-time and paid for by the certified. Heavy-metal and potency class actions are routine, and gray-market peptide vendors forge certificates of analysis (FDA warning letters to seven online sellers, Mar 2026). Honest brands cannot distinguish themselves.
ideas.solution: A claim registry. The brand states a specific, machine-checkable claim (for example lead below X per serving, or label potency within 10%), posts a $10-50k bond in escrow and accepts a protocol: retail-purchased units, an accredited lab, and blinded replicates. Challengers pay for tests or use subsidised credits, and a neutral panel confirms chain of custody. A failed claim pays the challenger and forfeits the bond and badge. A claim that survives N challenges earns a 'survived challenge' tier that retail buyers can query by API.
ideas.why_now: Finnrick has now published 10,000+ independent peptide tests, proving that crowds will fund lab tests of vendors. Heavy-metal exposés and lawsuits keep recurring. Stablecoin and card-hold escrow make small bonds cheap to run. Retailers want a liability shield for clean-label shelves.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5k annual listing fee, a 1-3% bond-management fee, challenge-processing fees, and retailer API licences.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Bug bounties worked in software because they turn hostile sceptics into paid auditors. Physical-goods certification does the opposite and pays friendly auditors. A bond makes the brand fund the scepticism, and only honest brands can afford to post one, which gives the badge a real price premium.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach 10 clean-label brands that already publish certificates of analysis (creatine, collagen, omega-3, kids' vitamins) and pitch it as cheaper than class-action defence. Sign one ISO 17025 lab for a fixed test panel. Run a public 'challenge week' with a supplement community, using a standard escrow account.

ideas.title: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data
ideas.one_liner: An audit that tells research buyers what share of their online-panel responses came from bots, agents or fraud farms, and recalibrates the study against a verified-human control sample.
ideas.customer: Insights heads at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms, UX-research teams, academic labs and pollsters who buy panel sample from third-party vendors at $5-500 per complete.
ideas.problem: One prompt to a commercial AI agent now passes screeners and attention checks. A controlled evaluation found synthetic respondents passing 99.8% of 6,000 attention-check trials. As little as 3-7% contaminated responses can invalidate conclusions. Panel vendors both sell the sample and score its quality, so buyers cannot trust the referee.
ideas.solution: A per-study data-quality audit. Response files (timings, paradata, device data, open-ends) go through a detection ensemble plus honeypot items. A subset of the same questionnaire goes to a small address-recruited, device-attested human panel as a ground-truth control. Deliver an audit stamp, contamination-adjusted estimates, and a vendor scorecard across suppliers.
ideas.why_now: Survey-fraud research in 2025-26 shows agents beating attention checks. An MIT-run $50K challenge is testing detection, and NORC published a fraud literature review. Election-season polling and pharma sample budgets raise the stakes, and buyers are asking who audits the panels.
ideas.revenue_model: $3-15k per study audit, $50-150k per year programmes for insights teams that spend $2-10M on sample, and vendor-scorecard subscriptions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Most anti-fraud tooling is sold by panel sellers, whose incentive is to under-report fraud. The scarce asset is not detection code but an independent, verified-human comparison group, because you cannot prove what is fake without a known-real reference.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit about 2,000 verified humans by address-based mail or a university survey-centre partnership. Buy sample from six panel vendors yourself and publish a 'state of sample quality' benchmark. Offer free audits to five insights leaders who have posted about bad data.

ideas.title: Cross-Lender Double-Pledge Registry for Receivables
ideas.one_liner: A hashed, shared ledger where lenders confirm that an invoice, receivable or auto loan has not already been pledged elsewhere, starting with freight and trade factoring.
ideas.customer: Independent factoring companies, ABL desks at regional banks, supply-chain-finance funds and private-credit lenders to mid-market suppliers.
ideas.problem: First Brands allegedly double- and triple-pledged about $2.3B of invoices. The SEC charged Tricolor's former CEO and CFO on 18 Aug 2026 with double-pledging subprime auto loans to multiple lenders and securitisations. No single funder can detect overlap because there is no mechanism for lenders to see each other's pledges, so small factors are hit constantly.
ideas.solution: Members submit hashed invoice fingerprints (debtor ID, invoice number, amount, date) by API and get 'clean' or 'conflict' back in seconds. Add automated debtor confirmation (email, portal and EDI checks that the invoice exists and where payment is directed) and remittance-diversion alerts. Use private set intersection or salted hashes so lenders never reveal borrowers, and a consortium contract plus UCC-style notice.
ideas.why_now: First Brands and Tricolor collapsed in Sept 2025, and DOJ (Jan 2026) and SEC (Aug 2026) actions followed. Private credit's growth, investor demands for collateral verification and bar-association guidance on being 'two-timed' have created board-level urgency.
ideas.revenue_model: $0.10-2 per query, $1-5k per month membership for small factors, $50k+ per year for funds, and $5-15 per automated debtor confirmation.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives in the gaps between lenders, not inside them. The data everyone needs (each other's pledges) is data nobody will share bilaterally. A neutral registry sells a network effect for detection, like Carfax or the UK's Cifas, rather than a better anomaly detector.
ideas.first_30_days: Start with freight factoring, where duplicate invoices and fake brokers are a known problem. Sign 10 independent factors and two fintech ABL lenders through industry associations, build the hashing API, and offer founding members a free tier in exchange for contributing data.

ideas.title: Proof-of-Review Receipts for AI-Using Professionals
ideas.one_liner: A tamper-evident record that a named, licensed human actually reviewed AI output, backed by planted-error vigilance tests, sold to firms and their malpractice carriers.
ideas.customer: Mid-size law firms, accounting firms and physician groups using AI drafting or scribes, and the malpractice and E&O carriers, MGAs and brokers underwriting AI use.
ideas.problem: Courts worldwide have issued about 1,490 decisions on AI-hallucinated filings (1,000+ in the US by May 2026), with sanctions up to $110k and the first suspensions. More than 60% of carriers now ask about AI use in underwriting, and some add AI endorsements or exclusions. Firms cannot prove that attorney review happened beyond a policy memo.
ideas.solution: A review layer (Word and Outlook add-in, EHR plug-in, browser extension) that logs what the AI produced, what the human changed, dwell time, automated cite-check results and sign-off. It also seeds a random slice of reviews with canary errors (a fake citation, a wrong dose in a test document) to measure whether reviewers really catch them. A signed monthly review-integrity report goes to the carrier for premium credit or endorsement eligibility.
ideas.why_now: AI-hallucination sanctions are growing by about eight cases a day. The EPIC 2026 claims survey shows carriers seeing more AI-related claims, and carriers are rewriting applications and endorsements now.
ideas.revenue_model: $30-80 per professional per month, carrier and broker partnerships (revenue share on premium credits), and a cite-check add-on.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The weak link is automation complacency, not just model hallucination. You can measure complacency the way airports measure screener vigilance, by planting known-bad items. Insurers will pay for measured human vigilance because it is a rating factor.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one legal-malpractice MGA or broker and 10 small firms (5-50 lawyers) through state-bar CLE channels. Ship a Word add-in that logs review and checks citations. Pilot canary errors with written consent.

ideas.title: Slop-Rating Feed for Kids' Filters
ideas.one_liner: A channel- and app-level data feed that classifies children's content as verified human-made, AI slop or unknown, sold to school web filters and kids' hardware.
ideas.customer: School-district web-filter and parental-control vendors, kids' tablet, audio-player and smart-speaker makers, and school districts directly.
ideas.problem: Fairplay found that 104 of the first 500 videos recommended to a fresh account were AI slop. On 1 Apr 2026 more than 200 organisations, including the American Federation of Teachers, asked YouTube to label and ban AI content on kids' surfaces, and YouTube said only that it is developing labels. Filters classify by topic (violence, adult), not by how content was produced.
ideas.solution: Continuously crawl kids-targeted channels, apps, audiobooks and games. Classify provenance using channel behaviour, voice and image-model signals, upload cadence and template reuse, plus human review. Add a 'verified human-made' tier through creator attestations and audits. Deliver category lists by API keyed on channel ID, domain or app package, plus teacher whitelist packs.
ideas.why_now: Spring 2026 investigations (NYT, Fairplay, CBC) and the April coalition letter made AI slop a school and parent issue. The EU AI Act's Article 50 labelling is beginning, and 1:1 school device fleets need a new filter category now.
ideas.revenue_model: $20-200k per year data licences to filter vendors, $0.10-0.50 per-device royalties from hardware makers, and $1-3 per student per year for districts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A platform's own AI label will always be optional and gameable. The buyer is whoever sits between the child and the platform, and they already buy category feeds. Selling a new dimension (provenance) into an existing distribution channel avoids consumer acquisition entirely.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a 20k-channel labelled seed set with three teacher or parent reviewers. Ship a free 'slop score' browser extension for teachers to collect signals and leads. Pitch three mid-size filter and parental-control vendors with a sample feed.

ideas.title: Integrity Desk for Grant Applications
ideas.one_liner: Cross-funder screening that catches AI-mass-produced applications, recycled proposals and forged partner letters before reviewers waste time.
ideas.customer: Community foundations, corporate giving programmes, state and regional economic-development agencies and accelerators, reached through grant-management platforms such as Submittable and Foundant.
ideas.problem: NIH capped principal investigators at six applications a year (effective 25 Sep 2025) after one applicant filed 40+ apparently AI-generated applications, and it says AI-developed proposals are not original work. Funders elsewhere see multiples of prior volume. Letters of support and partner commitments are the easiest thing to fabricate, and the same proposal is shopped to many funders.
ideas.solution: A plug-in and API for grant portals. It scores text reuse and AI boilerplate across applicants (including anonymised cross-funder fingerprints) and verifies claims and citations. It automatically calls back signatories of support letters for signed confirmation, checks entity registrations, tax status and beneficial owners, and keeps a shared duplicate-application registry across member funders.
ideas.why_now: LLMs drove the volume flood that prompted NIH's 2025 policy. Foundation staffing is thin, and federal and state scrutiny of grant fraud is rising.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25k per cycle for foundations, $0.50-5 per application via portal partners, and registry membership for funders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is the cURL lesson. When the cost of submission falls to zero, the reviewer's attention is the scarce resource. The winning move is not detecting AI text, which is unreliable, but verifying checkable third-party facts, like a partner's confirmation call, that AI cannot fake for free.
ideas.first_30_days: Run free pilot scans on last cycle's applications for three community foundations through regional grantmaker associations. Publish anonymised findings such as the share of applications with heavy text overlap. Pitch one grant-software vendor for a plug-in partnership.

ideas.title: FTC Review-Rule Audits for Franchisors
ideas.one_liner: Fixed-fee audits that find review gating, incentivised reviews and insider reviews across a franchisor's or dealer group's locations, and in the reputation vendors doing it for them.
ideas.customer: General counsel and marketing VPs at franchisors and multi-location operators (auto dealer groups, dental support organisations, home-services and fitness franchises), with reputation-management agencies as channel partners.
ideas.problem: The FTC Consumer Review Rule bans review gating, sentiment-conditional incentives, suppression and undisclosed insider reviews, with civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation. The FTC sent 10 warning letters in Dec 2025 and obtained a $4M order (partly suspended) in July 2026. Local operators often use review-request software that quietly routes unhappy customers away from public sites, and franchisors are exposed to franchisee behaviour.
ideas.solution: A 'Rule Ready' audit. Scan Google, Yelp, Facebook and vertical sites across all locations for suspicious bursts, employee reviews and incentive language. Mystery-shop vendors' review-request flows (does a 2-star responder get diverted from Google?). Deliver a risk-ranked location report and remediation playbook, then quarterly monitoring and a vendor certification for compliant review-request software.
ideas.why_now: Warning letters (Dec 2025), the first orders (July 2026) and law-firm commentary in mid-2026 show an enforcement pattern taking shape, and Italy's Mar 2026 Trustpilot fine shows the referee itself can be penalised.
ideas.revenue_model: $5-25k per audit scaled by location count, $2-8k per month monitoring, and certification fees from review-software vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Liability sits with the buyer of reputation software, not the vendor, and those vendors' flows were designed when gating was legal. The money follows the risk to the franchisor's general counsel.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one vertical, either dental support organisations or auto dealer groups. Cold-email 40 general counsel with a free three-location sample audit. Build scanners on public review data and line up two law firms as referral partners.

ideas.title: TAKE IT DOWN Desk for Small Platforms
ideas.one_liner: Outsourced 48-hour notice-and-removal operations (intake, requester verification, adjudication, audit logs) for forums, hosts and indie social apps.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size platforms with user-generated content (forums, image hosts, creator platforms, community apps, dating apps) that have no trust-and-safety staff, plus web hosts and their counsel.
ideas.problem: The FTC began enforcing the TAKE IT DOWN Act on 19 May 2026, wrote to 15 large platforms including Discord, Reddit and Automattic, and lists civil penalties of $53,088 per violation. Coverage reaches forums with user content. The 48-hour clock is real, but the request process is abusable, since false takedown notices can be weaponised, and platforms must verify that the requester is the depicted person without collecting more sensitive imagery.
ideas.solution: A hosted intake endpoint and a staffed desk. It offers identity-light requester verification (hash matching in the style of StopNCII), adjudication by trained reviewers with escalation, removal of known identical copies across the customer's site, an appeal and counter-notice path, and FTC-ready audit logs. Follow-the-sun contractors with wellness support provide coverage. Requires legal review per jurisdiction.
ideas.why_now: Enforcement started in May 2026, the FTC opened a complaint portal (TakeItDown.ftc.gov), and nonconsensual deepfake volume is rising. Small platforms cannot afford in-house teams, and the statute imposes a duty to act with no penalty for false requests.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-5k per month base plus $15-40 per resolved case, with enterprise SLAs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The statute mandates speed but not accuracy, so the operational risk is over-removal and abuse. The product is adjudication with a paper trail, not filtering, and the buyer's fear is an FTC letter, not a bad user.
ideas.first_30_days: Sell through forum-software hosting partners, web-hosting providers and indie creator platforms. Train a contractor pool in handling sensitive imagery and stand up intake for 10 pilot communities.

ideas.title: Court-Ready Deepfake Authenticity Reports for Lawyers
ideas.one_liner: $500-1,500, 48-hour forensic reports on disputed audio, video, screenshots and voicemails, written to survive an authenticity challenge.
ideas.customer: Solo and small family-law, employment and criminal-defence firms, insurer special-investigation units, and HR investigators.
ideas.problem: Cloned-voice voicemails and fabricated chats now appear in custody and harassment disputes. The proposed federal evidence rules on deepfakes (901(c)) and machine-generated evidence (707) have stalled, and in June 2026 the Standing Committee sent 707 back for further study, so judges decide case by case. Bespoke forensic experts cost $5-20k and take weeks.
ideas.solution: A productised workflow: intake with chain of custody, multiple detectors plus provenance checks (metadata, C2PA, compression history, device and source-app fingerprints), review and a signed declaration from a credentialed examiner, optional testimony, and template motions on authentication for lawyers.
ideas.why_now: Cheap voice cloning has moved from fraud into family and employment disputes. The federal rule process has stalled, leaving a gap that judges and lawyers must fill with experts, and lawyers face sanctions if they present unverified AI evidence.
ideas.revenue_model: $500-1,500 per report, $2-5k per day for testimony, and a $299 per month firm plan that includes three reports.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is weak everywhere. The scarce thing is a credentialed human willing to sign under oath with a documented method. Productise the signature and the paper trail, and treat detectors as inputs.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit three forensic audio and video examiners. Sell through local family-law bar associations and CLE talks. Publish three anonymised case studies and a report template reviewed by trial attorneys.

ideas.title: Green-Claims Clearance for EU-Bound Brands
ideas.one_liner: A crawl-and-fix service that strips or substantiates banned 'eco-friendly' and 'climate-neutral' claims on packaging, product pages and ads for brands selling into the EU.
ideas.customer: DTC brands, Amazon and Shopify sellers, and mid-size consumer-goods companies selling to EU consumers, plus their marketing agencies and EU authorised representatives.
ideas.problem: Directive (EU) 2024/825 applies from 27 Sept 2026. It bans generic environmental claims ('green', 'eco-friendly') without recognised excellent performance, bans offset-based 'climate neutral' claims, and restricts sustainability labels to certified or public schemes. Small brands have thousands of SKUs of copy across 24 languages and no clear way to check it.
ideas.solution: Crawl product pages, packaging PDFs and ad libraries, flag banned and risky patterns in 24 languages, and suggest compliant rewrites with evidence-pack templates (life-cycle summary, certification proof). Add a human legal-review tier and monitoring of competitors' claims for complaint filing.
ideas.why_now: The rule began applying on 27 Sept 2026, and member-state transposition laws are now in force. The separate Green Claims Directive was shelved, so consultancies shifted attention, yet this ban is already law and cheap to police by machine.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-5k initial audit, $300-1,500 per month monitoring, and agency white-label licences.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is a deadline-driven, per-SKU checking problem that suits software plus a thin human legal layer, and the first enforcement will often start with competitor complaints. The best lead-gen is showing a brand its own violations.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a claims lexicon in five languages. Scan the top 200 product categories on Amazon.de and .fr for violations. Email brand founders their own violations as a free preview. Partner with three EU marketing agencies.

ideas.title: Independent Verifier for LLM Inference Endpoints
ideas.one_liner: Continuous black-box testing that proves an API endpoint is serving the advertised model at the advertised precision, with a price-per-verified-quality index.
ideas.customer: AI-native companies and enterprises spending $50k+ per month on inference through routers, resellers and open-weights hosts, their procurement teams, and providers who want a 'Verified' badge.
ideas.problem: Endpoints can silently swap models, quantise or truncate context. Research on model substitution in LLM APIs (including an IRIS audit paper in July 2026) shows the problem is real, and a frontier lab's April 2026 postmortem acknowledged unadvertised changes that degraded output for weeks. No standard binds a response to a provider and model, so buyers cannot audit.
ideas.solution: Always-on probes from multiple regions using statistical fingerprints, random-string tests, tool-call accuracy and long-context recall. Alert on drift, publish a procurement dashboard of verified quality per dollar and a quarterly integrity leaderboard, and issue a 'Verified Endpoint' badge and SLA to providers.
ideas.why_now: Router and reseller markets exploded in 2025-26, margin pressure encourages silent quantisation, and agent workloads make small quality cuts expensive at scale. Fresh research gives credible detection methods.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-10k per month per buyer (scaled to spend), a share of verified savings, and $5-25k provider certification fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: This is a market for lemons. A 20% quality cut is invisible per request but material in aggregate, and the auditor's edge is statistical sampling at scale, not access to the provider.
ideas.first_30_days: Open-source the probe kit and publish a leaderboard across 30 endpoints serving the same open-weights model. Get five agent startups to run it, then convert to paid monitoring.

ideas.title: Blind Validation Enclaves for Clinical AI
ideas.one_liner: Confidential-computing sandboxes where a hospital's private patient data and a vendor's private model meet, and only a signed performance report leaves.
ideas.customer: Health-system AI governance committees and health-AI vendors (imaging, ambient scribes, risk models), plus payers and insurers of AI performance guarantees.
ideas.problem: Hospitals cannot validate vendor claims on their own patients because PHI cannot leave and vendors will not ship weights. Published metrics rarely transfer to local populations. The Joint Commission and the Coalition for Health AI issued responsible-AI guidance in Sept 2025 and planned voluntary certification, so buyers now need evidence.
ideas.solution: A managed enclave (confidential VMs and GPUs) deployed in the hospital's own cloud tenant. The vendor's container runs against local retrospective data. Attestation proves that the evaluation code was unmodified and nothing was exfiltrated. The output is a signed report on subgroup performance, calibration and drift, repeated quarterly as post-deployment monitoring.
ideas.why_now: Confidential GPUs became generally available on major clouds in 2025, health systems adopted ambient scribes and imaging AI at scale, and Joint Commission and CHAI guidance created a demand for third-party assurance. The vendor-paid validation model is visibly conflicted.
ideas.revenue_model: $25-75k per validation (split between hospital and vendor), $10k per quarter monitoring, and payer or insurer programmes.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Neither party trusts the other with its crown jewel, and the usual referee (the vendor) is conflicted. A machine that both sides can cryptographically verify replaces the trusted third party, so the product is the attestation as much as the test.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one academic medical centre's informatics team and two imaging or scribe vendors for a single use-case pilot. Use an existing confidential-computing offering rather than building infrastructure.

ideas.title: Provably Anonymous, Provably Employee Whistleblower Channel
ideas.one_liner: A reporting channel where a worker proves they hold a company email using zero-knowledge proofs, without the employer or vendor ever learning who they are.
ideas.customer: EU and UK employers with 50-500 staff that must run internal reporting channels, employment-law and compliance firms that deploy them, and works councils.
ideas.problem: Whistleblower-directive compliance is often a checkbox. Employees do not believe 'anonymous' hotlines that log IPs and identities, so use is low. Employers get junk or spoofed reports and cannot confirm that a reporter is a real current employee.
ideas.solution: ZK-email proofs of an employer-domain, DKIM-signed message let a reporter prove employment without revealing which mailbox. Per-report nullifiers block duplicates, and no identity is stored. Add anonymous two-way messaging, evidence upload, and a 'verified current employee in a group of at least 10' signal to the company. Independent cryptographic review is published.
ideas.why_now: ZK-email tooling is open source and maturing, EU digital-identity wallets are due by end 2026, and deepfake and spoofed reports are increasing. Whistleblower rules now apply to smaller firms, so many companies are buying cheap channels for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per company, with a 30% channel margin for law firms and a free tier for firms under 50 staff.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Hotline usage is limited by trust in anonymity, which promises cannot improve, only making identification cryptographically impossible can. The same proof gives employers what they want (verified employee) and gives hostile insiders nothing.
ideas.first_30_days: Prototype with open-source zk-email libraries. Line up three employment-law firms and 10 SMEs for a free pilot, and commission a small third-party cryptography review to publish.

ideas.title: Human Baseline Vault for AI Detection
ideas.one_liner: Proctored, ID-verified, unassisted human writing and speech, timestamped and sealed, sold first as ground truth for detector calibration and later as low-background evaluation data.
ideas.customer: AI-detection vendors, ed-tech firms and publishers, university integrity offices, trust-and-safety teams, and AI labs' evaluation teams.
ideas.problem: Studies report detector false-positive rates of 5-20% on native English and up to 61% on non-native writing. 25+ universities have restricted detectors, and a February 2026 New York court ordered Adelphi to expunge a student's AI accusation. Vendors cannot prove error rates by population because clean post-2022 human ground truth is unknowable, since everyone's 'human' data may be AI-assisted.
ideas.solution: Recruit 20k+ verified people across strata (non-native English, neurodivergent, technical, legal and academic writers, age bands) to write and speak in proctored sessions. Samples are timestamped and hash-anchored. Sell calibration sets and per-population false-positive certificates to detector vendors, then an annually refreshed vault as 'low-background steel' for evaluations and future disputes.
ideas.why_now: Over half of web traffic is automated and training and evaluation sets are increasingly contaminated. Lawsuits and university bans mean detector buyers now need error rates by population, and AI labs need uncontaminated human evaluation data.
ideas.revenue_model: $50-250k dataset licences, $20-75k per detector audit and certificate, and annual refresh subscriptions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Like pre-1945 steel free of nuclear fallout, verified pre-contamination human data gets more valuable every year, and its value lies in the chain of custody, not the text itself.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 500 participants through two university partners for a native versus non-native pilot. Pitch two detector vendors and one ed-tech firm. Publish an independent study on false positives by population to earn press.

ideas.title: Surety-Bonded License Plates for AI Agents
ideas.one_liner: A registrar that binds each autonomous agent to a legally accountable, insured principal through a surety bond and a revocable credential merchants and platforms can check.
ideas.customer: Agent developers and vendors that need acceptance by merchants, booking and B2B procurement platforms, the merchants and platforms that want to admit agents safely, and surety insurers or MGAs.
ideas.problem: Visa, Mastercard and Amex are activating agent payments in 2026, but dispute and liability infrastructure barely exists. Merchants bear the chargebacks, and Mastercard is reportedly planning scheme-carried liability for certified agents. Identity schemes such as Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Cloudflare's signed agents say who an agent is, but not who pays when it misbehaves.
ideas.solution: Register the agent and underwrite it with a test suite, spend caps and a behaviour policy. Issue a signed credential with a visible bond limit, and let merchants and platforms verify it with one API call. A claims process pays merchants for agent-caused losses, and violations revoke the credential. Start with an MGA and fronting-carrier partnership.
ideas.why_now: Card networks are moving on agent payments in 2026, Lloyd's-backed AI liability covers launched in 2025, and merchants are asking who is liable for agent orders. Signed-agent identity standards exist, so the missing layer is accountability.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual premium of 1-5% of bond limit, a registration fee, and float on the claims reserve.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Identity without liability is theatre. The mature trust machine for strangers who might not pay is suretyship (contractor licences, notary bonds), not a reputation score, and a bond turns 'trust me' into a price.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one vertical (restaurant and hotel booking, or B2B procurement agents). Sign five agent developers, secure a letter of intent from a surety or MGA, build the underwriting test suite, and get three merchants to trial a bonded-only allowlist.

ideas.title: Receipts-Only Reviews via Open Banking
ideas.one_liner: Reviews that only people who provably paid can post, with the payment verified through open-banking data and only merchant, amount band and month disclosed.
ideas.customer: UK and EU independent restaurants, salons, tradespeople and clinics (verified-review widget and profile subscription), with lenders, insurers and marketplaces as later data buyers.
ideas.problem: Trustpilot removed 4.5M fake reviews in 2024 and was fined by Italy in Mar 2026 for failing to verify authenticity. The FTC rule and UK consumer law ban fake reviews, and no platform can verify offline purchases. Merchants cannot prove their reviews are real, and review sites sell services to the businesses they rate.
ideas.solution: The reviewer links a bank through an open-banking account-information partner (such as TrueLayer or GoCardless). The app reads one transaction and produces a selective-disclosure attestation (merchant, amount band, month), then posts. Merchants get a '100% paid-customer reviews' widget and structured-data markup. Reviewers get neutral, sentiment-independent cashback funded by merchants.
ideas.why_now: Fake-review enforcement is intensifying (FTC warning letters Dec 2025, Italy's Trustpilot fine Mar 2026), the AI-generated review flood is growing, and AI shopping agents ingest reviews as trust signals. Open banking now has enough UK users to make linking a normal action.
ideas.revenue_model: GBP 19-49 per month merchant subscription, API and data licences to lenders and marketplaces, and float on cashback funding.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The referee problem vanishes when the proof comes from the bank, not the platform. A review site that sells to the businesses it rates can never be trusted, but a receipt cannot be bought.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 30 independent restaurants in one UK city, put a QR code at the till, and build on an open-banking partner's sandbox. Launch with local press as 'the review site you cannot buy'.

ideas.title: L-Band Radar Watchdog for Small Levee Districts
ideas.one_liner: Turn free NISAR L-band radar into monthly, engineer-stamped settlement and seepage alerts for the small local districts that own most of America's levees.
ideas.customer: Reclamation, levee and drainage districts (California Delta and Central Valley, Iowa/Illinois/Missouri/Arkansas drainage districts) and owners of small high-hazard earthen dams and irrigation canals. Budgets are $50k to $2M a year, run by a board plus a part-time manager.
ideas.problem: Grass-covered earthen levees lose coherence in C-band InSAR (Sentinel-1), so cheap remote settlement monitoring never worked on them. Districts rely on annual walk-through inspections by volunteers or consultants. Failures are catastrophic, and grant, subvention and insurance paperwork demands documented condition history that most districts lack.
ideas.solution: A pipeline on NISAR L-band (about 10 m, 12-day repeat, which sees through vegetation) plus Sentinel-1 and soil-moisture change. It produces per-levee-mile maps of slumping, settlement and unusual wetness (seepage proxy). Alerts go to a partner licensed geotechnical engineer, who signs a one-page condition letter. The district attaches that letter to state levee-subvention and federal rehabilitation-program files, insurer renewals and board minutes. The dashboard is secondary; the stamped trigger is the product.
ideas.why_now: NASA/ISRO began releasing NISAR L-band data free through ASF DAAC on July 20, 2026 (acquisitions from June 17, 2026; full science record due by end of 2026). Tens of thousands of levee miles are locally owned, and nobody had L-band time series at this cadence before. Whoever starts the baseline now owns the longest history.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription of $3k to $8k a year per district, tiered by levee miles. Add $1.5k to $4k per engineer-stamped event report. Later, portfolio-level data licences to flood insurers and reinsurers, and to state agencies that fund many districts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The radar data is free and commoditizing, so the data is not what the customer buys. They buy a defensible, professionally signed trigger that unlocks grant money, satisfies insurers and shifts liability. The moat is the engineer-of-record relationship, local ground truth and a baseline archive that starts accumulating today.
ideas.first_30_days: Process Sentinel-1, ALOS-2 and the first NISAR stacks over one Delta island or Iowa drainage district with a known past slump, to show a retrospective catch. Sign a geotech firm as engineer of record. Offer 5 districts a free baseline map and a $1.5k pilot, pitched at levee-district association and flood-board meetings. Aim for 2 paid pilots by day 30.

ideas.title: Persistent Methane Plumes as Equipment Sales Leads
ideas.one_liner: Sell satellite-detected methane emitters to the vendors who profit from fixing them: a lead-gen engine, not a compliance tool.
ideas.customer: Vapor-recovery-unit makers, flare-gas-to-power microturbine and genset vendors, landfill gas-collection contractors, dairy digester and RNG developers, and small gas gatherers or offtakers. Roughly 2,000 companies in the US; first buyers are sales VPs at 20-person equipment firms.
ideas.problem: Abatement vendors prospect blind at trade shows. Emitters are often unaware of a persistent leak or vent, or they do not know its dollar value. A 500 kg/h plume is roughly 230,000 MMBtu a year, or about $0.7M of saleable gas at $3/MMBtu. Methane data today is sold to regulators, ESG buyers and the emitters themselves, and none of them are motivated.
ideas.solution: A weekly ranked lead list of persistent emitters, defined as repeated detections across passes from open Carbon Mapper, EMIT and Tanager plume products, with GHGSat tasking to confirm the best leads. Each lead joins the plume to facility ownership (state permits, landfill and EPA datasets), wasted-gas value per year, distance to pipeline or grid, and likely fix type. Delivered as a CRM feed plus a one-page dossier.
ideas.why_now: Plume data is now abundant and partly free: Carbon Mapper's Tanager publishes public plume products, and GHGSat is expanding to 16+ satellites. With US federal methane-penalty pressure pushed out, pitches built on fines are weak, while pitches built on recovering saleable gas still work. Cheap gas-to-power gensets and microturbines are also more available.
ideas.revenue_model: $2k to $6k a month per vendor per basin or vertical. Success fee of 2% to 4% of first-year equipment or service revenue on closed leads, capped. Later, sell offtake and RNG-interconnect leads to gas buyers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats a methane plume as a violation to be reported. It is really an unmonetized commodity with a known street address and a quantifiable price. Selling the plume to the person who profits from fixing it inverts the market and does not depend on regulation.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull open plume data for the Permian, Appalachia and Ohio/Pennsylvania landfills and build the top 100 persistent emitters. Hand-verify ownership and gas value on each. Cold-offer 25 equipment vendors and landfill gas contractors three free leads, then $3k a month. Ask for a paid pilot from 3 by day 30.

ideas.title: Weather Forecasts for GPS Jamming
ideas.one_liner: A crowd-sensed, forecastable map of GNSS jamming and spoofing for the civil operators nobody warns: survey and RTK fleets, drone operators and marine underwriters.
ideas.customer: First: commercial drone operators, RTK survey and construction machine-control fleets, and precision-ag contractors in the Baltics, Poland, Finland, Turkey and the Gulf, at $99 to $499 a month. Second: marine war-risk MGAs, P&I clubs and route planners, at $50k to $250k a year.
ideas.problem: Jamming and spoofing have surged (EASA revised its GNSS-interference bulletin again in July 2026; Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb dominate ship incidents; insurers are bracing for mega-claims). Operators learn about it when a drone flies away or autosteer fails. Public maps such as GPSJam are daily averages built from ADS-B, too coarse for a specific field or route hour.
ideas.solution: A sensor network of cheap multi-band GNSS receivers and opted-in Android raw-GNSS phones (hosts are farmers, truckers and drone pilots, paid in free forecasts). It detects carrier-to-noise collapse and spoofing signatures at about 1 km resolution in near real time. On top of that sits a forecast (jammers repeat by hour and geometry) and an API/SMS alert such as 'L1 degraded within 20 km of your flight plan 14:00-16:00'. A signed position-integrity report is offered to insurers.
ideas.why_now: Dual-frequency GNSS chips cost about $10 and expose raw measurements. Android exposes raw GNSS data. Jamming intensity rose sharply through 2025-26, and insurers and P&I clubs have started buying authentication tech, so the demand signal is visible in the market.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS of $99 to $999 a month for fleets. Annual data licences of $50k to $250k to insurers and MGAs. Per-report fee for integrity certificates. Optional hardware host kit sold at cost.
